The Epistle Dedicatory

Right Honorable, among all the societies and states of which the whole world of mankind has consisted, from the first calling of Adam in Paradise to this day, the first and most ancient is the family. For if we look into the Scriptures, the writings of Moses, which in time go beyond all the histories and records of men, plainly declare that it was the will of God to sanctify that first joining of Adam and Eve as the root in which man’s whole posterity was contained in virtue and power, and from which, in the ages that followed, both church and commonwealth were to spring and grow to their perfection. And all those nations and countries before the Flood, whose heads descended in a direct line from the first two houses of Seth and Cain, had no outward form of civil government by which they were ruled, nor any visible face of a church to which they belonged. The whole frame of their government, both civil and ecclesiastical, was confined within the bounds of private families. And from the Flood onward, the house of Noah became the common mother in which the other two states were contained, and out of whose womb they issued afterward as posterity multiplied, in number equal to the stars of the sky and the sand on the seashore.

The verdict of the heathen on this point has answered to the voice of Scripture. Some of the1 learned among them have called the family2 the first society in nature, and the ground of all the rest. Others again have compared it to the beehive, which we call the stock, in which many swarms are bred that fly out from it into the world, to raise and maintain other states.3 Others, not unfitly, liken it to a metropolis, or mother city, which first trains up her native inhabitants and then4 moves some of them to other places to live, where they may be formed as members, to live in obedience to the laws of their head.

Since the family is in this way the seedbed of all other societies, it follows that its holy and righteous government is a direct means to the good ordering of both church and commonwealth. Yes, its laws, rightly informed and religiously observed, help to prepare and dispose men to keep order in other governments. That is why the Holy Spirit, in the book of the Scriptures, has in great wisdom commended both rules for direction and examples for imitation to husbands and wives, to parents and children, to masters and servants, in every point of Christian conduct toward God and man. For this first society is, as it were, the school in which the principles of authority and subjection are taught and learned. And just as the superior who fails in his private charge will prove unfit for public employment,5 so the inferior who has not been trained in a course of subjection in the household will hardly bear the yoke of civil obedience.

Again, the corruption or decline of this first government must of necessity lead to the ruin of the rest. For an error in the foundation puts the body and every part of the whole building in plain danger. In the old world, before the Flood,6 though “all flesh had corrupted their ways,” yet the first source of that universal flood of sin came out of the household state, and from there it spread into the whole earth. It was the fault of the private government of Eli the priest that turned his sons Hophni and Phinehas7 from wicked children into ungodly churchmen. It was David’s error in the running and guidance of his own house8 that encouraged his sons Absalom and Adonijah,9 presuming on their father’s indulgence,10 to become bad citizens of the commonwealth,11 and to aspire to the kingdom and usurp it by plots and practices of rebellion.

To forbear further instances of this kind: from due consideration of what has been said, I hold it both necessary and profitable for people of every rank to be thoroughly informed of the right way of setting up and ordering the private state of the family, so that they may be furnished with fit grounds for the common good in more public and open courses. For this end the present discourse of Christian Economy was first composed by the author, and it is now thought fit to be published for the instruction and edification of the multitude. It commends itself by its shortness and clearness, both of which, applied to the understanding and the memory, may give satisfaction to every well-disposed reader. And it also has a kind of eminence above other treatises of this nature published before, in various respects.

First, experience teaches that the questions of conscience in matters of marriage are very many in number and difficult in nature. Here we will find either direct answers to some of them, or at least the grounds for resolving various cases, warranted by the word, in such a way that, on trial, little or nothing that bears on the reader’s satisfaction will appear to be left untouched.

Secondly, the main aim of the author in its several branches is to make plain this truth in particular: that no family can have a share in the blessing and favor of God which is not founded in his fear and ordered according to his revealed will. It is true that the heathen, in their writings on the same subject,12 show that nature by her dim light may give some good directions to this purpose, and that merely natural men have prospered in practicing the virtues of household government. Yet the true happiness of houses and their inhabitants depends wholly on the special grace of God, and comes out of his promise; and that promise is directed only to those “who fear the Lord, who walk in His ways,”13 for it is godliness alone that holds “promise for the present life and for the one to come.”14 Therefore to dream of a blessing in any other state that is not seasoned with godliness and ordered by the direction of divine law is only witless presumption. For the family itself, from which they grow, has no further assurance of blessedness than it has right and title in the promise.

Lastly, it contains here and there some special grounds of truth that serve to uncover various errors of popish doctrine in points belonging to marriage, namely these:

  1. That this state is free to all men, even to those who have the gift of self-control; and for those who do not have the power to abstain, it is expressly enjoined by God as necessary.15 This uncovers the error of forbidding it absolutely to some sorts of men, without the least exception made for their ability to abstain. And in this case, though the Church of Rome prescribes help by prayer and effort where the gift is lacking, yet here she adds two more absurdities to the former. She imposes by her laws a necessity of abstaining where God has given liberty by his word; and she makes men flee from the only remedy that he himself has sanctified to another, which he neither commands by his will nor encourages by promise.
  2. That marriages consummated without the free and advised consent of parents, either explicit in words or implicit by tacit allowance, are utter nullities in the court of conscience. This doctrine is cleared in this book both by Scriptures and by the consent of antiquity. In it the Jesuits’ proposition is challenged, that the consent of the parties alone is sufficient16 ad Matrimonium firmum ac ratum efficiendum [to make a marriage firm and ratified]. So also is that decree of the Council of Trent17 which professes to detest clandestine contracts, and yet in the same breath pronounces the curse of anathema on those who affirm that parents may ratify or make void marriages contracted by their children without their allowance.
  3. That marriage lawfully begun and consummated is made void only by way of divorce in the case of adultery. So says our Savior:18 “anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality,” etc. And this liberty granted by Christ, both to dissolve the marriage and to marry again, cannot be restrained or cut off by any human ordinance. This point is directly attacked by two other rules of that council. One is that the Church of Rome does not err when she teaches (as they profess,19 Iuxta Euangelicam & Apostolicam doctrinam [according to the doctrine of the Gospel and the apostles], but in truth in express contradiction to it) that the knot of marriage cannot be broken because of adultery, and that neither party may undertake to marry again during the life of the other after the putting away. The other is that the vow of chastity and entering into holy orders has force to loose the bond of marriage. And in this case separation is made and allowed de facto [in fact] by the sole authority of the Pope, even though the party who stays settled in the marriage refuses to consent.
  4. That the judgment and determination of matrimonial causes (contracts and their impediments, degrees of kindred, divorces, and the like) rests originally in the civil magistrate. It is in his power to ordain and establish laws concerning them, agreeable to God’s word, and to have them put into execution. For this purpose, in doubtful and difficult cases, the20 ancient church did not rest absolutely on her own decrees, but had recourse to the seat of justice, especially under Christian magistrates, submitting herself to their laws and constitutions in that kind. The21 Church of Rome, by contrast, has determined that these causes belong simply and only to ecclesiastical judges. And therefore she has concluded that marriage is a sacrament, so that the deciding of marriage cases, becoming on this ground an action of a spiritual nature, might be transferred from the civil courts to their spiritual courts. By their own constitutions, the sovereignty of those courts in these affairs is greatly enlarged. For though they admit that civil princes have some right in them, yet the princes must hold it22 in subordination to the authority of the church magistrate; and when the governor of a province makes a law on this, he must do it approbante Principe Ecclesiastico, by the allowance of the Pope; otherwise his laws are utter nullities. And among their reasons of policy, one of the chief is this: that by this means they might raise a profit for the See of Rome by the sale of their dispensations.

Now these points, together with the substance of this small discourse, I gladly commend to your Lordship, desiring that under the wings of your honorable protection it may walk safely out in the world, to the view and benefit of others. The true report of your long-standing love of the truth, and of your favorable inclination toward its ministers and dispensers, has encouraged me in this; all the more because the subject fits in some measure your present state. For God has adorned your house with olive plants,23 a virtuous and hopeful offspring, whose young years, seasoned in it by the sweet savor of their father’s virtues, may in time yield a plentiful increase of honor in this commonwealth, and so advance your name in themselves and their posterity. To this may be added my own desire to give some testimony of duty to your Lordship, holding it your due to be held in honorable esteem among men, since your care has been to maintain the honor of the Most High by your constant profession and practice of religion. And so, emboldened by the persuasion of your Lordship’s favor and acceptance, I humbly take my leave, and commend you to the grace of24 God, who is able to build you up further and give you an inheritance among those who are sanctified. Finchingfield, September 26, 1609.

Your Lordship’s, to be commanded in all Christian duty,

THO. Pickering.

1. Of Christian Economy, and of the Family

Christian Economy is a doctrine of the right ordering of a family.

The only rule for ordering the family is the written word of God. By it David resolved to govern his house, when he says, “I will walk in my house with integrity of heart” (Ps 101:2). And Solomon affirms that “by wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established” (Prov 24:3).

A family is a natural and simple society of certain persons who have a mutual relation to one another, under the private government of one. These persons must be at least three, because two cannot make a society. And above three, under the same head, there may be a thousand in one family, as there are in the households of princes and men of state in the world.

2. Of the Household Service of God

A family, for its own good state, is bound to perform two duties: one to God, the other to itself.

The duty to God is the private worship and service of God, which must be established and settled in every family. And the reasons for this are these.

First, because this duty stands by the express commandment of God, who by his apostle says, “I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension” (1 Tim 2:8).

Again, it is confirmed by the custom and practice of holy men in their times. “For I know him,” says the Lord concerning Abraham, “that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord by doing what is right and just, in order that the Lord may bring upon Abraham what He has promised” (Gen 18:19). To the same purpose Joshua speaks: “But if it is unpleasing in your+ sight to serve the Lord, then choose for yourselves+ this day whom you+ will serve, whether the gods your+ fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you+ are living. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord!” (Josh 24:15). And Cornelius is reported to have been such a man: “He and all his household were devout and God-fearing” (Acts 10:2).

Thirdly, common reason and equity show it to be a necessary duty. For the happy and prosperous state of the family, which consists in the mutual love and agreement of the husband and wife, in the dutiful obedience of children to their parents, and in the faithful service of servants to their masters, depends wholly on the grace and blessing of God; and this blessing is joined to his worship. For 1 Tim 4:8: “Godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come.” Ps 127:1: “Unless the Lord builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the Lord protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain.” v. 2: “In vain you+ rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat—for He gives sleep to His beloved.” v. 3: “Children are indeed a heritage from the Lord, and the fruit of the womb is His reward.” Ps 128:1: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in His ways!” v. 2: “For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours.” v. 3: “Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house, your children like olive shoots sitting around your table.” v. 6: “May you see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel!” 1 Sam 1:27: “I prayed for this boy,” says Hannah, “and the Lord has granted me what I asked of Him.”

The household service of God has two parts. The first is talking together on the word of God, for the edification of all the members of the family to eternal life. The second is calling on the name of God, with giving thanks for his benefits. Both of these are commended in the Scriptures. Deut 6:6: “These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your heart.” v. 7: “And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.” v. 20: “In the future, when your son asks, ‘What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the Lord our God has commanded you+?’” v. 21: “Then you are to tell him, ‘We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.’” v. 24: “And the Lord commanded us to observe all these statutes and to fear the Lord our God.” Ps 14:1: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” v. 4: “They do not call upon the Lord.”

The times of this service are these:

The morning, in which the family, coming together in one place, is to call on the name of the Lord before they begin the works of their callings.

The evening also is another time to be used in prayer. For the family has seen the blessing of God on their labors through the day, and now the time of rest draws on, in which every one is to commend his body and soul into the protection of the Lord. For no man knows what will befall him before he rises again; nor does anyone know whether he will ever rise again or not. It is therefore a reckless boldness to go to rest without praying.

Besides these, there are other times also in which to perform this duty, as before and after meals. For food and drink are blessed to those who receive them by the word and prayer. 1 Tim 4:4: “For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected, because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.”

Now the word of God approves these times. Deut 6:7: “You shall … speak of them … when you lie down and when you get up.” Ps 55:17: “Evening, morning, and noon I pray and cry out, and He hears my voice.” Ps 127:2: “In vain you+ rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat,” unless the Lord grants a blessing, “for He gives sleep to His beloved.”

To these may at times be added the exercise of fasting, which is to be used, as occasion requires, both publicly and privately; especially when those of the family are called to it by some present or impending calamity. Esth 4:16: “Go and assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day, and I and my maidens will fast as you+ do. After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!” Zech 12:11: “On that day the wailing in Jerusalem will be great … The land will mourn, each family on its own: the family of the house of David on its own, and their wives on their own; the family of the house of Nathan on its own, and their wives on their own,” etc.

Families in which this service of God is performed are therefore, as it were, little churches, yes, even a kind of paradise on earth. For this reason St. Paul, writing to Philemon, greets “the church that meets at your house” (Phlm 2). And in the same way he sends greetings to the church of Corinth from Aquila and Priscilla, “and so does the church that meets at their house” (1 Cor 16:19). On the other side, where this duty of God’s service is not practiced, but is either for the most part or altogether neglected, a man may call those families no better than companies of profane and godless atheists. As they deny God in their hearts, so they are known by this mark, that “they do not call upon the Lord” (Ps 14:4). Yes, such families are fitly compared to a herd of swine, always feeding greedily on the acorns, but never looking up to the hand that beats them down, nor to the tree they fall from.

The other duty, which concerns the house itself, is that every member of the family, according to their ability, employ themselves in some honorable and profitable business, to maintain the temporal state and life of the whole. Gen 3:19: “By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground—because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.” 1 Cor 7:20: “Each one should remain in the calling he had when he was called.” Now if anyone in the family turns aside from his calling and entices another to idolatry, he is to be exposed (Deut 13:6). And again, their case is very fearful who do nothing in their houses but dress finely and dine daintily from day to day. This is the black mark that Scripture sets on the rich glutton, Luke 16:19: “Now there was a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen, who feasted sumptuously every day.”

3. Of Married Folks

A family is divided into various combinations, or couples, of persons.

A couple is that by which two persons, standing in mutual relation to each other, are joined together, as it were, into one. And of these two, the one is always higher and bears rule; the other is lower and yields subjection.

Couples are of two sorts: principal, or less principal.

The principal is the couple of married folks; and they are so called with respect to marriage.

Marriage is the lawful joining of the two married persons, that is, of one man and one woman, into one flesh. Such was the first institution of marriage (Gen 2:21). It is expounded by our Savior Christ, Matt 19:6: “So they are no longer two, but one flesh.” And also by Paul, Eph 5:31: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined25 to his wife” (as two boards are joined together with glue) “and the two will become one flesh.” Therefore this is an eternal law of marriage, that two, and not three or four, shall be one flesh. And for this reason the fathers of old who had many wives and concubines, though it may be that through custom they sinned in ignorance, are yet in no way to be excused.

Marriage in itself is a thing neither commanded nor forbidden, and the kingdom of God consists no more in it than in food and drink. And yet it is a state in itself far more excellent than the condition of single life. For first, it was ordained by God in Paradise, above and before all other states of life, in Adam’s innocence before the fall. Again, it was instituted on a most serious and solemn consultation among the three persons of the holy Trinity. Gen 1:26: “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness, to rule over …” Gen 2:18: “Jehovah Elohim also said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper.’” Thirdly, the manner of this joining was excellent, for God joined our first parents Adam and Eve together directly. Fourthly, God gave a large blessing to the state of marriage, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth.” Lastly, marriage was made and appointed by God himself to be the fountain and seedbed of all other sorts and kinds of life, in the commonwealth and in the church.

Now if mankind had continued in the uprightness and integrity it had by creation, the state of single life would have had no value or esteem among men; nor could it have had any place in the world without great contempt of God’s ordinance and blessing.

Nevertheless, since the fall, single life is in many respects far better than marriage for some men who have the gift of self-control; yet not in itself, but only because of circumstances, in regard to the various calamities that came into the world by sin. For first, it frees a man from many great cares of household affairs. Again, it makes him much more fit and disposed to meditate on heavenly things without distraction of mind. Besides that, when dangers in matters belonging to this life are either present or impending, the single person is happy in this case, because he and his are more secure and safe than others who are in the married state. 1 Cor 7:8: “Now to the unmarried and widows I say this: It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am.” v. 26: “Because of the present crisis, I think it is good for a man to remain as he is.” v. 28: “But if you do marry, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. But those who marry will face troubles in this life.” v. 32: “I want you+ to be free from concern.”

The end of marriage is fourfold.

The first is the procreation of children, for the propagation and continuance of the seed and posterity of man on the earth. Gen 1:28: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it.” Gen 9:1. 1 Tim 5:14.

The second is the procreation of a holy seed, so that the church of God may be kept holy and chaste, and there may always be a holy company of men to worship and serve God in the church from age to age. Mal 2:15: “Has not the Lord made them one, having a portion of the Spirit? And why one? Because He seeks a godly seed.”

The third is that, after the fall of mankind, it might be a sovereign means to avoid fornication, and so to subdue and quench the burning lusts of the flesh. 1 Cor 7:2: “But to avoid sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.” v. 9: “But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.” For this reason some schoolmen err, who hold that the private coming together of husband and wife cannot be without sin unless it is done for the procreation of children. Lombard, the Master of the Sentences, says the contrary, namely, “that marriage before the fall was only a duty, but now since the fall it is also a remedy.”

The fourth end is that the married parties may by it perform the duties of their callings in a better and more helpful way. Prov 31:11: “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value.” v. 13: “She selects wool and flax and works with eager hands.”

Marriage is free to all orders and sorts of men without exception, even to those who have the gift of self-control; but for those who cannot abstain, it is, by the express commandment of God, necessary. Heb 13:4: “Marriage is honorable among all, and the marriage bed undefiled.” 1 Cor 7:9: “But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry.”

From this it appears to be a clear case that the commandment of the Pope of Rome, by which he forbids marriage to certain persons, namely the clergy, is purely diabolical. For so the apostle writes, 1 Tim 4:1: “Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons,” v. 3: “They will forbid marriage.”

But various things are alleged against this doctrine.

Objection 1. The apostle commands the married among the Corinthians to abstain by consent for a time, “so you+ may devote yourselves+ to fasting and prayer” (1 Cor 7:5). I answer that Paul does not speak in that place of the daily and common service of God in prayer, but of the solemn and extraordinary exercise of it, which was joined with fasting and abstinence in common dangers and calamities.

Objection 2. 1 Cor 7:32: “The unmarried man is concerned about the work of the Lord, how he can please the Lord. But the married man is concerned about the affairs of this world.” Answer. The place is not to be understood universally, of all, but only of some: of those married persons who are carnal and fleshly. And he who is married is to be so concerned for the things of the world that he ought to have, and may have as well, a special regard for the things that concern God and his kingdom.

Objection 3. 1 Tim 5:11: “The younger widows,” says the apostle, “will want to marry, and thus will incur judgment because they are setting aside their first faith.” Answer. By “the first faith” Paul means the promise and vow they made to Christ when they were baptized. And they are said there to “begin to grow wanton against Christ” by denying or renouncing that faith, and not otherwise.

Objection 4. If a man earnestly and from his heart asks for the gift of self-control, God will give it to him; and therefore he need not marry.

Answer. The gifts of God are of two sorts: some are general, some are particular. General gifts are those that God gives generally to all, and these may be obtained if they are asked lawfully, according to God’s word. Jas 1:5: “Now if any of you+ lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.” v. 6: “But he must ask in faith, without doubting.” Particular gifts are those given only to certain men. Of this sort is the gift of self-control and the like, which, though they are often and earnestly asked for, are yet seldom or never granted to some men. This appears in Paul’s example, who, being buffeted by Satan, says of himself, “Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me. But He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you’” (2 Cor 12:8, 9).

25. προσκολληθήσεται

4. Of the Contract

Marriage has two distinct parts: the first is its beginning; the second, its accomplishment or consummation.

The beginning is the contract, or betrothal; the end or accomplishment is the solemn declaration of the contract, by what we properly call marriage. Deut 20:7: “Has any man become betrothed to a woman and not married her? Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man marry her.” Matt 1:18: “His mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, but before they came together, she was found to be with child through the Holy Spirit.”

Between the contract and the marriage there ought to be some certain space or distance of time. The reasons for this may be these:

First, a business of such great importance as this should not be attempted rashly or unadvisedly, but should rather be done by degrees, in process of time, according to that saying, not so ancient as true:26 Actions of weight require mature deliberation before resolution. Secondly, that during such a space inquiry may be made whether there is any just cause that may hinder the consummation of the marriage. For before the parties come together, what is amiss may be remedied and amended, which will be too late to do afterward. Thirdly, in these cases persons betrothed must have regard to decency as well as to necessity: not seeking at once, upon the contract, to satisfy their own fleshly desires after the manner of brute beasts, but proceeding in it with mature deliberation.

The contract is a declaration, or mutual promise, of future marriage, made before fit and qualified judges and witnesses.

The best way of giving this promise is to make it27 in words concerning the present time, and simply, without any exception or condition, expressed or conceived. For by this means the bond is made the surer, and the ground or foundation of the future marriage is better laid. And it is on this ground alone that persons betrothed are called husband and wife in Scripture. Jacob, speaking of Rachel, who was only betrothed to him, says to Laban, “Grant me my wife” (Gen 29:21). Deut 22:23: “If there is a virgin betrothed to a man, and another man encounters her in the city and sleeps with her, you+ must take both of them out to the gate of that city and stone them to death—the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he has violated his neighbor’s wife.” Matt 1:20: “Joseph … do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife.”

Now if the promise is uttered in words28 for time to come, it does not strictly bind the parties to performance. For example, if one of them says to the other, N., I will take you, etc., and not N., I do take you, etc., by this form of speech the match is not made, but only promised to be made afterward. But if, on the other hand, it is said, N., I do take you, and not I will take you, by these terms the marriage is begun at that very instant: though29 not in regard of fact, yet in regard of the right and claim that the parties have in each other, in deed and in truth. And this is the common opinion of the learned. Yet nevertheless, if the contracting parties say to each other, I will take you to, etc., with the intention of binding themselves at the present, the bond is strictly made in conscience before God, and so the contract is indeed made30 for the present time before God. It is true that he who keeps the promise he has made, as far as lies in him, does well. Yet if the promise has or carries with it some just cause why he should afterward change his purpose, the contract expressed in terms for time to come, though it was made earlier and confirmed by oath, must nevertheless give place to the contract made for time present.

Betrothals made on a condition that is honorable, possible, and belonging to marriage cease or remain pending just so far as the condition attached ceases or remains pending. For example, one party may promise to marry the other on condition that his or her kinsman consents to the match, or on condition of a dowry that she is to bring him, suitable to her upbringing and the family she comes from. As these conditions are kept or not kept, the promise likewise stands or does not stand.

But conditions that are necessarily understood, or that can certainly be kept and come to pass, neither hinder nor suspend marriage. Such as this: I promise you marriage, if I live; or, I promise to marry you, if the sun rises tomorrow.

Again, conditions that are either impossible or dishonorable are not to be counted as promises attached31 in the way of marriage. Of this sort are these: I will be your wife, if you will take wings and fly; or, If you will bring about a miscarriage.

Furthermore, if the betrothed parties lie together before the condition (though honorable and belonging to marriage) is performed, then the contract for time to come is, without further controversy, sure and certain. For where there has been carnal use of each other’s body, it is always presupposed that mutual consent concerning marriage has gone before.

26. Diu deliberandum quod semel statuendum [Long must be the deliberating over what is to be settled once for all].

27. In verbis de praesenti.

28. In futurum.

29. Non de facto, de iure.

30. De praesenti.

31. In fauorem Matrimonij [in favor of marriage].

5. Of the Choice of Persons Fit for Marriage

To make a contract, two things are required: first the choice, and then the consent of the parties.

Choice is an inquiry after persons who are marriageable.

Persons marriageable are those who are fit and able for the married state.

This fitness or ability is known and discerned by certain signs, which are either essential to the contract or accidental.

An essential sign is one without which the contract in hand becomes an utter nullity. And of this sort there are principally five.

The first is the distinction of the sex, which is either male or female. The male is man, of a superior sex, fit for procreation. The female is woman, of an inferior sex, fit to conceive and bear children. 1 Cor 11:7: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man.” 1 Tim 2:12: “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.” By this distinction is condemned that unnatural and monstrous sin of uncleanness between parties of the same sex,32 commonly called sodomy; and also the mixing of the33 kinds of creatures, when one kind commits filthiness and abomination with another.34

The second sign is the just and lawful distance of blood.

Distance of blood is just and lawful when neither of the persons who are to be married comes near to the kindred of their flesh, or to the flesh of their flesh. For so the Scripture speaks, Lev 18:6: “None of you+ shall come near to any of the flesh of his flesh,” or to “the kindred of his flesh.”35 Here it is to be observed that by a man’s flesh is meant that substance which is of himself, or of which he himself consists. And by the flesh of his flesh is meant that which next and immediately issues out of the flesh of which he consists. From this it follows that the touching or coming near of flesh to flesh is not spoken of strangers, but of those only who are of kindred.

Kindred is of two sorts: kindred by blood (consanguinity), or kindred by marriage (affinity).

Kindred in consanguinity are those who issue from one and the same common blood or stock. And there are certain degrees by which kinsmen of this sort are distinguished from one another.

A degree is a generation or descent between two persons who are of the same blood. For one person alone cannot make a degree, unless he is considered in relation to another, in regard of generation.

Now many degrees continued or derived from one and the same head make a line. And a line is twofold: the direct line, or the crosswise line, commonly called the collateral.

In the direct line, count how many persons there are, and there are so many degrees, leaving out only the person who is in question in the case at hand, and from whom we begin the count.

  • Abraham.
  • Isaac.
  • Jacob.
  • Joseph.

Here Joseph is three degrees distant from Abraham, Jacob two, Isaac one, or the first.

The direct line is either ascending or descending.

The direct line ascending is the lineage of all the ancestors, and it has several degrees. Of the first degree are the father and the mother. Of the second, the grandfather on both the father’s and the mother’s side, that is, the father of my father and the father of my mother; and the grandmother, that is, my father’s mother and my mother’s mother. Of the third, the great-grandfather, or the father of my grandfather; and the great-grandmother, or the mother of my grandfather. Of the fourth, the great-grandfather’s father, and the great-grandfather’s or great-grandmother’s mother. Of the fifth, the great-grandfather’s grandfather, and the great-grandfather’s or great-grandmother’s grandmother. Of the sixth, the great-great-grandfather’s grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather’s or great-great-grandmother’s grandmother.

The direct line descending is the lineage of a man’s own posterity. And it also has several degrees. The first is the son and the daughter; the second, the grandson and the granddaughter; the third, the grandson’s son and the granddaughter’s daughter. The fourth is the grandson’s grandson, or the son in the fourth degree of lineal descent, and the granddaughter’s granddaughter, or the daughter in the same degree of descent. The fifth is he and she who are three lineal descents from the child’s child. And so on with the rest in their order, by whatever names they are called and known.

Now in this direct line, whether ascending or descending, the person about whom the case or question is raised comes near to the kindred of his flesh. And therefore marriages in this line are prohibited without end, without any limit; so that if Adam himself were alive now, he could not marry by the law of God, because he would come near to the kindred of his own flesh, as Moses speaks. The reason for this is that in the direct line, superiors and inferiors are to each other as parents and children. And since the kinship between parents and children is the first and nearest of all, their union in marriage must be most unclean, and contrary to nature.

The collateral or crooked line is the one that runs alongside the direct line, whether ascending or descending, in the ranks of the kindred. And it is either unequal or equal.

The unequal is the line in which the person in question and his kinsman are unequally distant from the common stock, or head of the kindred.

And in this line, as many degrees as the kinsman who is furthest off is distant from the common stock, so many degrees are he and the kinsman in question distant from each other.

For example,

  • Terah.
    • Abraham—
    • Nahor
      • Bethuel
        • Laban.

Here Laban, being removed furthest off, that is, three degrees from the common stock Terah, is likewise three degrees distant from Abraham, his great-uncle, and Abraham as many from him.

Furthermore, kinsmen in this line are of two sorts: some are superiors to the person in question, and some are inferiors to him.

Superiors are those who are akin to his father and mother, on one side or the other; and that either nearer or further off.

Those who are closely akin to them are these.

  1. The uncle on the father’s side, or the father’s brother; the aunt on the father’s side, or the father’s sister. The uncle on the mother’s side, or the mother’s brother; the aunt on the mother’s side, or the mother’s sister.
  2. The great-uncle, or the grandfather’s brother; the great-aunt, or the grandfather’s sister. The great-uncle, or the grandmother’s brother, and the great-aunt, or the grandmother’s sister.
  3. The great-uncle on the father’s side, or the great-grandfather’s brother; and the great-aunt on the father’s side, or the great-grandfather’s sister. The great-uncle on the mother’s side, or the great-grandmother’s brother; and the great-aunt on the mother’s side, or the great-grandmother’s sister.
  4. The great-grand-uncle on the father’s side, or the great-grandfather’s father’s brother; and the great-grand-aunt on the same side, or the great-grandfather’s father’s sister. The great-grand-uncle on the mother’s side, or the great-grandmother’s mother’s brother; and the great-grand-aunt on the same side, or the great-grandmother’s mother’s sister.

Now these, in regard of their inferiors, stand in the place of parents, and therefore they come near to the kindred of their flesh.

The superiors who are distantly akin to the parents on one side are these.

  1. The son and daughter of the great-uncle or great-aunt on the father’s side, or of the great-uncle or great-aunt on the mother’s side.
  2. The grandson and granddaughter of the great-uncle or great-aunt on the father’s side, or of the great-uncle or great-aunt on the mother’s side,36 near to the first cousin.

And these, as they stand compared with their inferiors, do not come near to the kindred of their flesh.

The equal collateral line is the one in which kinsmen are equally distant from their head.

Kinsmen of this line are:

  1. Whole brothers, that is, brothers by the same father and mother; or half brothers, that is, brothers by the same father but not by the same mother. Again, whole sisters by the same father and mother, or half sisters by one of them and not by both.
  2. The children of brothers, or first cousins: that is, the uncle’s sons or daughters, or the aunt’s sons or daughters. The children of sisters, or first cousins: that is, the aunt’s sons or daughters, who are the children of two sisters.
  3. The cousin who is the son of the great-uncle on the father’s or mother’s side, and the cousin who is the son of the great-aunt on the father’s or mother’s side. The cousin who is the daughter of the great-uncle on the father’s or mother’s side, and the cousin who is the daughter of the great-aunt on the same sides.

In this line, as many degrees as the party in question is removed from the common stock, twice as many degrees is he removed from his kinsman in question. Take the case between Bethuel and Isaac, as in this example.

  • Terah
    • Abraham—
      • Isaac.
    • Nahor
      • Bethuel.

Here Bethuel, being two degrees removed from Terah, is four degrees distant from Isaac.

Now he who is in the second degree of this line comes near to the kindred of his flesh; and for that reason the marriages of brothers and sisters are unlawful and forbidden.

But several things are alleged against this.

Objection 1. The sons of Adam, who were the first brothers in the world, married their sisters. Marriages in this degree may therefore seem to be lawful. Answer. The case of those persons in those times was a case of necessity, which could not be avoided, and so it was warranted by divine dispensation. For God had given them his own express commandment in this matter: “Be fruitful and multiply” (Gen 1:28). Besides this, there were then no other women in the world by whom they might have offspring and posterity, but only their sisters. From this it is plain that God’s will was to permit them to take even their sisters as their wives. But now, outside this special dispensation from God, such matching is utterly unlawful, being an open breach of another express commandment given afterward by God himself (Lev 18:9, 11). To this purpose Augustine says, in answer to the example put forward,37 “The practice of those first times was then backed by urgent necessity; the more ancient it was, the more damnable it proved afterward, when it was restrained by God’s commandment.”

Objection 2. Sarah was Abraham’s sister, and yet Abraham took her as his wife. Gen 20:12: “She really is my sister, the daughter of my father—though not the daughter of my mother—and she became my wife.” Gen 11:29: “Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. Abram’s wife was named Sarai.” Answer. On this instance there are several opinions. The Jews grant this much: that she was called by a name common to all kinswomen, namely a sister, yet she was in fact Abraham’s niece, the sister of Lot and the daughter of Haran, Abraham’s brother, whom Moses elsewhere calls Iscah (Gen 11:29). Others think that she was stepdaughter to Terah, Abraham’s father, because Abraham himself says, “She is the daughter of my father, not of my mother.” Others are of the opinion that she was Haran’s stepdaughter, and after his death was taken into the family of Terah, her grandfather, who also stood in the place of her father, now dead; and so she was called his daughter. Now however hard it is to find certain truth amid this variety of judgments, this is beyond doubt: that God in those days tolerated many things which nevertheless he did not altogether approve.

Objection 3. 2 Sam 13:13: Tamar says to her brother Amnon, “Please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.” Answer. The speech of Tamar is not to be taken simply, as if she desired what she said, or as if what she wished him to do were lawful to be done. She only sought to put him off by giving him this advice, for her own deliverance from the danger she was in at that moment. Or at least it may be said that she wrongly supposed it was lawful for the king to grant such a request, if her brother Amnon had made it to him. Whichever way this speech is taken, nothing such as is claimed can be gathered from it.

Now beyond the second degree of the equal collateral line, it seems that those who are joined to one another in marriage do not touch the kindred of their flesh. And therefore the law of God does not forbid first cousins, that is, the children of brothers and sisters, to marry.

Indeed, if examples carry weight here, the Scripture approves such marriages. For it is written that Jacob married Rachel, the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother (Gen 28:2). Again, that “Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to their father’s brothers’ sons” (Num 36:11). And “Othniel son of Caleb’s brother Kenaz captured Kiriath-sepher, and Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage” (Josh 15:17).

However, in this case the rule of the apostle is to be followed: that nothing be done, even in things that are otherwise lawful, by which a man’s brother may stumble, or be offended, or made weak (Rom 14:21). Therefore it is fitting that such marriages should not be made, because at times they may give offense in regard of the law of the magistrate, and because they come somewhat near to the bounds and limits of blood and stock which God has set down in his word. Augustine, in the fifteenth book of De ciuitate Dei, ch. 16, says to this purpose, Experti autem sumus, etc. That is, “We have found by experience how rarely custom has admitted those marriages between first cousins, because of the nearness of blood they have to the degree of brothers and sisters, though such marriages were warranted by the laws, since the law of God has not forbidden them, nor as yet the law of man. Nevertheless the practice, lawful in itself, was forborne all the more because it came near to what was unlawful; and so marriage with a first cousin seemed in a way to be marriage with a man’s own brother or sister, etc. However, there is no question that in these times it has been well provided by laws that such marriages should not be undertaken. For not only is the multiplying of alliances hindered by them; this harm also grows from them: the friendship and love which affinity procures between men who are strangers cannot be enlarged and increased where men do not go outside the limits and bounds of their own blood. Indeed, there is naturally in man a commendable measure of natural shame, by which, considering nearness in blood, he acknowledges a due debt of modesty and honor to his nearest kindred; and so he restrains himself, in regard of them, from the occasions and acts of concupiscence to which he is inclined in respect of others. And this is why, generally, the modesty that ought to be in those who intend marriage avoids, as much as it can, these and similar unions.” The same is the judgment of Ambrose in one of his letters to his friend Paternus,38 in which he dissuades him from marrying his son to his first cousin, on the grounds alleged above by Augustine. Ambrose adds this as well: that though it were lawful in itself, being nowhere forbidden by God, yet being inexpedient in several respects, it ought not to be done, according to the saying of the apostle, “Everything is lawful for me,39 but not everything is expedient.”

But it is maintained on the contrary that God by express law forbids marriage with the aunt, the father’s sister (Lev 18:12), and with the mother’s sister (v. 13), and with the father’s brother’s wife, who is also the aunt (v. 14). Therefore, by the law of proportion, he forbids marrying the children of these persons. For in nature it is a settled case: if a man may not marry the mother, much less may he marry the daughter.

Answer. The argument is faulty and concludes nothing to the purpose. For the reason is not the same in both. In the direct line of consanguinity, those who are sisters to the father and mother stand in the place of parents, and their nephews and nieces are to them as children. Therefore marriages among them can stand by no law, whether of God, of nature, or the positive laws of nations. It is not so with first cousins. For since they have no such relation, there is in their marriages, by the law of Moses, no uncovering of nakedness, nor any breach of public propriety. The blessing of God on some of them mentioned in Scripture, as on Jacob and Rachel and others like them, plainly shows that such marriages were lawful in themselves and pleasing to him. And so much concerning kindred by blood, or consanguinity.

Kindred in affinity is that by which the bounds of two kindreds are brought into the fellowship of one and the same family; or by which persons who are not of one blood are allied to each other by marriage. That is why it is called affinity: because it joins into one the bounds of kindreds which before were apart.

Affinity, or alliance, grows by a mingling or sharing of blood, in the joining of man and wife together in lawful marriage. For a bare and simple contract does not properly make alliance between the parties; marriage does, after the contract is finished and consummated.

Again, the same alliance ceases and ends at the death of either party, betrothed or married; yet the prohibition of union in marriage remains and stands in force, for the preservation of public propriety.

Now there is a kind of likeness and proportion between kindred by blood and kindred by marriage, not only in regard of degrees and line, but also in respect of the prohibition of degrees.

Those who are of alliance are commonly brought under these heads.

  1. The father-in-law, or the husband’s or wife’s father. The mother-in-law, or the husband’s or wife’s mother.
  2. The mother’s husband, or stepfather to those born of another man. The father’s wife, or stepmother to those born of another woman.
  3. The wife’s father’s father, or grandfather, and the wife’s mother’s mother, or grandmother; that is, the grandfather and grandmother of the wife.
  4. The son-in-law, or daughter’s husband, and the daughter-in-law, or son’s wife.
  5. The granddaughter’s husband, and the grandson’s wife.
  6. The stepson, that is, the son of a man by another wife, or of a woman by another husband. The stepdaughter, that is, the daughter of a man by another wife, or of a woman by another husband.
  7. The stepson’s son, that is, the son of him who is a man’s son by another woman, or a woman’s son by another man. And the stepdaughter’s daughter, that is, the daughter of her who is a man’s daughter by another woman, or a woman’s daughter by another husband.
  8. The husband’s or wife’s brother, and the husband’s sister, or brother’s wife.
  9. The sister’s husband, and the brother’s wife.

Concerning affinity, I propose these rules.

I. In whatever degree a man is of consanguinity to a wife, in the same degree of affinity he is to the wife’s husband. And the reverse. For example:

  • Isaac
    • Esau.
    • Jacob.
      • Joseph—
    • Joseph
  • Samuel
    • Aaron.
    • Eli.
      • Maria.
    • Levi.

Here, if Mary, Joseph’s wife, is two degrees distant from Esau, Joseph’s uncle on the father’s side, then Joseph himself is also two degrees distant from Aaron, the brother of Eli his father-in-law. If Mary the wife is one degree distant from her own father Eli, and two from her grandfather Samuel, then her husband is also one degree distant from Eli his father-in-law, and two from Samuel his wife’s grandfather. Another example:

  • Herod.
    • Herod.
    • Philip, whose wife is Herodias.

Here, since Herod is in the first degree of consanguinity with his brother Philip, Herodias, his brother’s wife, is in the first degree of affinity to him.

II. Rule. Kin by marriage within the degrees, both of the direct and the collateral line, come near to the kindred of their flesh in the same way that kin by blood do in the same lines; and the like degrees in both are forbidden. Therefore in the direct line of affinity it is just as unlawful for the father-in-law to marry the daughter-in-law, or the son-in-law to marry the mother-in-law, as it is for the father to marry the daughter, or the son the mother. Again, in the collateral line, it is as unlawful for the uncle on the mother’s side to marry the wife of his sister’s son (and so in other degrees) as it is for him to marry in the same degrees of consanguinity. The reason is that in these lines, as well as in those of consanguinity, superiors and inferiors are to each other as parents and children.

From this, among other things, it may be gathered that it is in no way lawful for a man, when his wife is dead, to marry her sister. Lev 18:16: “You must not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife; it is your brother’s nakedness.” And Lev 20:21: “If a man marries his brother’s wife, it is an act of impurity. He has uncovered the nakedness of his brother.”

Against this doctrine it is objected, first, that God commands a man not to take a wife together with her sister during her life (Lev 18:18). In that place, it is said, he does not simply forbid a man to marry two sisters one after another, but to marry them both together; and therefore, after the wife is dead, a man may marry her sister.

Answer. The place is a flat prohibition of the sin of polygamy. For in the Hebrew idiom, to take a wife to her sister is nothing else than to take two wives, one to another. The same form of speech is used elsewhere by Moses, as in Exod 26:3.

“Five of the curtains are to be joined together,” [the woman to her sister] that is, one to another; “and the other five are to be joined” [the woman to her sister] that is, the one to the other. Ezek 1:9: “Their wings were joined” [the woman to her sister] that is, the one to the other. Again, Moses himself there gives two reasons against polygamy. The one is that the man is to love, cherish and comfort his wife; whereas if he took to himself another besides her, he would greatly vex his first, lawful wife. The other is that by this means he would uncover the nakedness of his wife; that is, he would deal very dishonorably with her to whom he was lawfully married before.

Objection 2. The Lord commanded by a special law that if a man’s brother died without offspring, he should take his brother’s wife and raise up offspring for him (Deut 25:5).

Answer. The words of Moses are a special exception to a general law set down in Lev 18:16: “You must not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife; it is your brother’s nakedness.” And they are directed particularly to the Israelites, for a special cause: that when the elder brother died without offspring, the name of the firstborn might not be blotted out, but the family might be preserved in that name by raising up offspring for him. Since this was a privilege belonging only to the Israelites, on that special ground, it must not be extended to any other sort of men whatever. Nor is the text to be understood only of more distant kinsmen, as some think, but also of the nearest of the kindred by blood. This appears plainly from the history of Ruth, in these words of Naomi to her daughters-in-law (Ruth 1:11): “Return home, my daughters. Why would you+ go with me? Are there still sons in my womb to become your+ husbands? Return home, my daughters. Go on, for I am too old to have another husband,” etc.

III. Rule. The wife’s kinsman by blood is of affinity to her husband only; but to the husband’s kindred by blood that kinsman has no affinity at all. So, the other way, it is true that though the husband’s kinsman by blood is allied to his wife, yet he has no alliance to those who are her kinsmen by blood. The reason is that between the kindred by blood on the man’s side and the kindred by blood on the woman’s side there is no affinity. For the prohibition of the degrees of affinity has force only in those who are the cause of it, and goes no further. Now since the cause lies only in the married persons themselves, the effect may not reasonably be extended to those who are of the same blood with either of them.

From this rule it follows that the kindred by blood of both married persons may lawfully marry one another. The stepson may marry the daughter of his stepmother. A father, and his son by another wife, may marry a mother and her daughter. Two brothers may lawfully marry two sisters.

IV. Rule. Kindred of affinity to the wife40 are also kindred of affinity to her husband. But how? Not strictly, but only in a certain sense, and as it were of affinity. So also the other way: kindred of alliance to the husband are, as it were, of alliance to his wife. For example, the wife of my father-in-law, who is not my wife’s own mother but her stepmother, is, as it were, my mother-in-law. For she is, as it were, of affinity to me, because she is truly of affinity to my wife.

Those who are of affinity only in a certain sense cannot fittingly marry one another. And therefore the son-in-law may not marry his wife’s stepmother, because, being of affinity to his wife, she stands in the place of a mother-in-law to him. Nor may the daughter-in-law marry her husband’s stepfather, because he is, as it were, a stepfather to her. Again, my sister’s husband may not marry my brother’s wife, for they are in a certain sense brother and sister to each other. The reason for this is that the wife is held in law to be a41 part of her husband; and therefore, if affinity hinders marriage with one of the married couple, it equally hinders marriage with the other, in the like case and respect.

And so much concerning the distance of blood, which must most necessarily be observed in choosing persons fit for marriage. For in the eighteenth chapter of Leviticus there are sixteen different sorts of persons with whom marriage is forbidden. The first is the mother. The second is the stepmother. The third, the sister by the same father and mother. The fourth, the half sister, by one of the parents only. The fifth is the granddaughter by the son. The sixth, the granddaughter by the daughter. The seventh, the father’s sister. The eighth, the uncle’s wife, that is, the father’s brother’s wife. The ninth, the mother’s sister. The tenth, the daughter-in-law, or son’s wife. The eleventh, the brother’s wife. The twelfth, the wife’s mother. The thirteenth, the stepdaughter, that is, the wife’s daughter by another husband, or the husband’s daughter by a former wife. The fourteenth is the stepson’s daughter, that is, the daughter of him who was the wife’s son by another husband. The fifteenth, the stepdaughter’s daughter. The sixteenth is the wife’s sister. And not only these, but all others that answer to them, in the same or a like degree, are by equal proportion forbidden to be taken in marriage.

It is alleged that the prohibitions mentioned in that chapter are merely Mosaic, that is, ceremonial, and therefore do not bind us now in the New Testament.

Answer. That is a flat untruth, as will appear by these reasons.

First, the Canaanites, long before these laws were given by Moses to the Israelites, were grievously afflicted for breaking and despising them. This may be gathered from what is written in the same chapter of Leviticus,42 v. 3: “You+ must not follow the practices of the land of Canaan … You+ must not walk in their customs.” And v. 24: “Do not defile yourselves+ by any of these practices, for by all these things the nations I am driving out before you+ have defiled themselves.” v. 25: “Even the land has become defiled, so I am punishing it for its sin, and the land will vomit out its inhabitants.”

Secondly, the prophets themselves after Moses are accustomed to count these prohibitions not ceremonial but moral. Ezek 22:10: “In you they have uncovered the nakedness of their fathers; in you they violate women during their menstrual impurity.” Amos 2:7: “A man and his father have relations with the same girl and so profane My holy name.”

Thirdly, the same laws are also urged in the New Testament, in which the legal ceremonies came to an end and were finished. Mark 6:18: John said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!” 1 Cor 5:1: “It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you+, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife.”

Fourthly, nature itself, by its own instinct, abhors such unions, and the prohibitions of them have sufficient ground even in her principles. It is for this reason that, in all ages, not only the laws of the Roman emperors, but also the civil canons and constitutions of men very skilled in that field, have been expressly made against such persons as have offended in those unions forbidden by the law of Moses.

Fifthly, the Lord himself has threatened many great punishments to be inflicted for breaking these same laws. Lev 20:11: “If a man lies with his father’s wife, he has uncovered his father’s nakedness. Both must surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.” v. 12: “If a man lies with his daughter-in-law, both must surely be put to death. They have acted perversely; their blood is upon them.” v. 14: “If a man marries both a woman and her mother, it is depraved. Both he and they must be burned in the fire.” v. 17: “If a man marries his sister, whether the daughter of his father or of his mother, and they have sexual relations, it is a disgrace. They must be cut off in the sight of their people.” v. 20: “If a man lies with his uncle’s wife, he has uncovered the nakedness of his uncle. They will bear their sin; they shall die childless.” Deut 23:2: “No one of illegitimate birth may enter the assembly of the Lord, nor may any of his descendants, even to the tenth generation.” Deut 27:20: “Cursed is he who sleeps with his father’s wife.”

The third essential sign of a person marriageable is ability and fitness for procreation. And this, in a holy and modest way, is always presumed to be in the party contracted, unless the contrary is plainly known and discerned by some evident infirmity in the body.

From this I gather that it is unlawful to make a contract with a person who is unfit for the use of marriage, either by natural constitution of body or by accident: for example, by reason of sickness, or of frigidity, or of incurable palsy, or lastly of the loss of the parts belonging to generation. These and similar impediments have force, even if a contract has already been made, to make it an utter nullity. For God makes known his will in them: that he does not approve of such a betrothal, but would have it dissolved.

Again, a contract made between two persons who are43 under age is to be held and counted unlawful. And even if it is made by the consent or command of parents, it is of no weight. This always holds, unless it is ratified by a new consent of the parties after they come of age, or unless they have in the meantime had private and carnal intercourse with one another.

Again, take the case that two are betrothed, of whom one is under age and the other of full age. The party of full age ought to wait and look for the time when the outcome of the betrothal already made may be seen. And the one under age may not break off consent, either before or when he or she comes of age, but must wait for the fulfillment of the contract when he or she is out of minority.

The fourth essential sign is a sound and healthy constitution of body, free from incurably contagious diseases.

From this it follows that a promise of marriage made between two persons, one of whom has a disease so loathsome that the other, on good ground, cannot possibly endure familiar fellowship and company with him, is utterly unlawful, even though the disease does not wholly hinder the use of the body.

Of this sort are leprosy, syphilis, and the like. For there cannot be any marital use between those who are tainted with such contagious diseases without evident danger of infecting each other, and those also who keep company with them, and others. Indeed, by this means the offspring of their bodies, growing from a corrupted seed, are born to lifelong misery, and to the great hurt and hindrance of the commonwealth. So the case is plain: such marriages cannot be undertaken with a good conscience.

Now if one party has a disease which, though not contagious, is either incurable or so44 loathsome that the other has just cause to loathe his company (for example, if he is sick of a lethargy, of epilepsy, or similar diseases), then it is lawful to marry him, because such a contract is not expressly forbidden, nor is it plainly hurtful to the commonwealth. Yet it is not expedient. For since the disease is loathsome to the sound party, the marriage also will become unprofitable, and that party will be in danger of breaking the commandment of the Moral law in which God forbids adultery.

The fifth essential sign of a person marriageable is freedom from marriage, by which both parties who enter the contract are so at liberty that neither the man has another wife at present, or is promised to another, nor the woman has another husband, or is promised to another. The reason is that God himself counts that marriage alone lawful in which one man is joined to one woman, and they both into one flesh. And so he judges it unlawful for one man to have more wives than one, and equally for one woman to have more husbands than one at the same time.

From this it follows that it is against the law of God, and the first institution of marriage, for a contract to be made between persons of whom one is already betrothed to another. For as long as the first promise stands in force, the man can no more be betrothed to two women than he may be the husband of two wives. For the betrothed woman, by the bond of her promise to the man, becomes a wife; and the man, by the bond of his promise to the woman, becomes a husband (Deut 22:23, 24).

Again, there can be no betrothal, and so no marriage, with one who either has been divorced without sufficient cause, or has wrongfully forsaken and rejected a lawful mate before. To this purpose our Savior Christ says in Matt 19:9: “I tell you+ that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman, commits adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.” And Saint Paul, 1 Cor 7:11: “But if she departs, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.”

So far I have treated the essential marks, which belong to the being of marriage. Now I come to those that are accidental.

An accidental mark of a person fit for marriage is one which belongs not to the being of marriage but to its well-being, that is, to the holiness and purity of that state. And of this sort there are three principal ones.

The first is parity or equality in regard of the Christian religion. For in marriage special care must be taken that believers are matched with believers, and Christians with Christians; not believers with infidels, or Christians with pagans. For the first kind of marriage alone, and always, is to be made and kept; the second is to be avoided, and indeed prohibited by positive laws and constitutions, the breach of which in such cases is to be severely punished. The neglect of this point was one principal cause of the destruction of the old world by the flood. Gen 6:2: “The sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose.” Abraham observed it in the marriage of his son Isaac, and for that purpose took an oath of his servant. Gen 24:3: “I will have you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and the God of earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I am dwelling.” And following that holy example, Isaac also gives a charge to his son Jacob: “Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women” (Gen 28:1). Afterward an express law of God was given by Moses concerning the Gentiles who lived in that land. Exod 34:15: “Do not make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land,” etc. Verse 16: “And when you take some of their daughters as brides for your sons, their daughters will prostitute themselves to their gods and cause your sons to do the same.” And the same law was urged by Ezra the priest in his time. Ezra 10:11: “Separate yourselves+ from the people of the land and from your+ foreign wives.” Lastly, Saint Paul exhorts the Corinthians, 2 Cor 6:14: “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers.” And Titus 3:10: “Reject a heretic after a first and second admonition.”

But suppose it happens that the betrothal is already made, and that both parties were believers at first, or only one of them; or that at first both were unbelievers, and afterward one of them is converted to the faith; or further, suppose that both were believers at the contract, yet some time after, one of them becomes an infidel, that is, a Jew, a Turk, or an obstinate heretic who denies the faith and razes even the very foundation of religion. What is to be done in this case? Surely even such a betrothal, once made and completed, if there are no other impediments but these, is to stand and continue firm and unchangeable, as long as the unbelieving party willingly yields and submits himself or herself to the performance of the marriage duties that properly belong to man and wife. My reason is the saying of Paul: “If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her.” Again: “And if a woman has an unbelieving husband and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him” (1 Cor 7:12, 13).

It may be alleged here that the sin of adultery dissolves the bond both of contract and of marriage, and therefore idolatry or unbelief does so much more, being a sin far more detestable than adultery. I answer that the question is not which of these is the greater sin, or more heinous in the sight of God (for in both respects unbelief far exceeds the other), but which of them is more contrary to the nature and condition of marriage. Now the sin of adultery is the only one that breaks the bond and renounces the faith pledged in marriage, and is the true cause of a divorce; idolatry or unbelief is not.

The second note is parity or equality in regard of age and condition.

First, of age. For though the marriage of persons whose years are far unequal is not expressly forbidden in the word, yet it agrees with the rules of expediency and decency that the aged should marry the aged, and the younger the younger.

The reasons are these. First, because by this means the comforts of this fellowship will likely always be equal, and so bring the more contentment to either party. Secondly, these unequal marriages often give offense to others. Thirdly, in some cases they cannot but prove troublesome even to the parties themselves. For when a man of great years marries a very young woman, or a young stripling marries an aged woman, the elder party, growing weak and impotent, may the sooner become unfit for marriage duties; and the younger, being of greater strength and ability, is the more in danger of being exposed to sexual incontinence, and that in the highest degree, unless restrained by God’s special grace. For this reason it was a great fault with which one Apuleius was justly charged: that while he was only a very young man, he was married to a wife sixty years of age.

Secondly, of condition and standing. For this also answers to the apostle’s rule, who exhorts men to think on and to do those things which are “true … right … admirable … of good report” (Phil 4:8). So it is a seemly and commendable practice that the prince, the nobleman, the freeman, the gentleman, the yeoman, and so on, should be joined in fellowship with those who are of the same or a like condition with themselves, and not otherwise. For this reason the ancient Romans are greatly to be commended, who (as we read in their histories) had such careful regard to their marriages in this respect that they made laws and constitutions to restrain inequality of worldly standing in such unions, by this means preventing much confusion and disturbance in families and in other orders of men. With this agrees the saying of Tertullian,45 “If a free woman had betrothed herself to a man who was another’s slave, and, after being warned of it three times by the one who had authority over her, still persisted in her purpose, she should by the law lose her freedom.”

The third note is public propriety and good name, by which the contract made becomes a matter of good report, well thought of and spoken of widely. “Whatever is of good report … think on these things” (Phil 4:8). From this I gather:

I. It is an unseemly thing for a man to make a promise of marriage to a woman who has been deflowered before, or who has been, or is, or may be convicted of adultery and uncleanness. Indeed, I add further that a contract made with one whom the man himself has deflowered before is unlawful by the law of God. For by divine law the adulterer and the adulteress should be put to death and cut off from human society (Lev 20:10).

II. It is altogether inexpedient for a woman to be married to a man who has a concubine, unless he first renounces her and testifies to it by true and unfeigned repentance. The reason is plain. Such a marriage cannot be undertaken in the Lord. And the man himself, having been polluted with his concubine before, now becomes an adulterer by marrying another; and she who is married to him gives consent to his adultery by this act of hers.

III. No man professing the Christian religion, much less a minister of the word, ought to take in marriage a harlot, a woman of ill fame, or one who comes of infamous parents, even though she is repentant. Lev 21:7: “A priest must not marry a woman who is a prostitute or profaned,” that is, one who has an evil name, or comes of disgraced parents. This law was in part ceremonial and Levitical, and so far abrogated. Yet since it has something moral in it, in that its reason (namely, because it is a reproach to a Christian, but especially to a minister) is still in force, it is to be held perpetual. For the profession of the Christian faith and the ministry of the church are chiefly to be respected, and whatever may harm their dignity and good name is to be avoided.

Objection 1. The prophet Hosea was commanded to take to himself a harlot: “Go, take a prostitute as your wife” (Hos 1:2). Answer. Hosea did not do it in deed, but in type and figure. For God commanded him in his prophecy to take on himself, as it were, the person of a fornicator, so that by this means he might the more effectually charge and convict the Israelites of their unclean and unchaste conduct.

Objection 2. The Lord also forbids the priest to marry a widow (Lev 21:14). It may seem inexpedient, therefore, for a minister to do so. Answer. The law about marrying a virgin and not a widow was not laid on all priests, but only on the chief priest (Lev 21:10). And he too might marry a widow, but only one who had been the widow of a priest, and no other (Ezek 44:22). Now this was commanded them for a special reason. For the high priest was a type of Christ, and Christ was in time to come to call his church, the elect, from among the Gentiles, and to marry them as a virgin betrothed to himself. Indeed, he was also to marry his church as a widow, but the widow of a priest only, because he was to gather to himself the remnant of the church of the Jews; yet not all of them, but only those who came of the holy fathers, and were Israelites not according to the flesh but according to the promise.

IV. It is not fitting for a man to be contracted to the sister of the woman who is already betrothed to him.

And so much for the first point required to make a contract, namely, the choice of a person fit for marriage.
