6. Of Consent in the Contract

The second thing required for making a contract is the free and full consent of the parties, which is indeed the very soul and life of the contract. And this consent consists in the approval, or (as we commonly call it) the Sure-making, of the parties contracted.

Consent in this case is twofold: either of the man and the woman, or of their parents.

As to the first: that the man and the woman may give free consent to each other, it is necessary that their judgment be sound, in respect of understanding, and that their choice be free, in regard of will. And here various cases are to be resolved.

I. Case. When the contract does not flow from the will and good liking of the parties, but is forced and compelled, what is to be done then?

Answer. Suppose the betrothal has been made through force or fear: I mean such force or fear as may fall on a constant and resolute man, and which has been brought to bear with full knowledge and deliberation. Then it is of no weight, and in truth an utter nullity, because it lacks the free and voluntary accord and assent of both parties. Nevertheless, if afterward the parties come to a new consent, or both yield to a later acceptance of what was made before, the betrothal will then stand in force, without further exception or contradiction.

II. Case. But what if consent has been given, and in process of time it appears to the betrothed persons that they have erred, either in choice, or in consent, or in both?

Answer. There is a threefold error in consent: the first of the person; the second of the ability, or estate, of the person; the third of the quality.

Error in respect of the person is when one person is taken for another, or when the contract is made between two, one of whom was taken to be such a party as he afterwards proved not to be. Now where this error is committed, it is a plain case that there was no consent. And therefore the contract, once this is certainly known, is wholly void. For the knowledge of the party is the ground of consent, and so belongs to the very substance of marriage.

Nevertheless, if the parties, once the error is known, have had private union with one another, and have either consented again or come to a later acceptance of the consent made before, the contract may stand, and does stand, in full force. For example, Jacob, by Laban’s deceit, had taken Leah as his wife in place of Rachel. So says the text, Gen 29:23: “When evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob, and he slept with her.” And v. 25: “When morning came, there was Leah!” Now by the judgment of the best divines, Jacob might justly have renounced Leah if he had wished, because Laban had given her to him as Rachel and so deceived him. Yet he would not use extremity, but kept her as his wife.

If it is said that there was an error in the person, and therefore no consent, and so Leah was not his lawful wife, but Rachel was, I answer that Jacob renewed his consent afterward. And that renewed consent, following on their knowing one another, made her his wife, though in strict rigor she was not. Again, Rachel was indeed the party to whom he was betrothed by the former contract; and therefore, upon their mutual agreement afterward, she also became his wife. So says the Holy Spirit, v. 27: “Finish this week’s celebration, and we will give you Rachel also in return for another seven years of work,” etc. v. 28: “And Jacob did just that … and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.”

Error of the ability or estate is when one of the parties, to whom the other gave consent, was taken to be rich and wealthy, and in the end proves to have been very poor, and not able to maintain that state of life.

As to this error, it must be considered whether the contract was made absolute, for the present time and so forever afterward, or conditional, for time to come only. If it was absolute, that is, framed in terms of the present time, then the deceit, though very offensive to the party deceived, and though on his complaint it ought in equity to be punished by the magistrate, yet has no force to break off the contract. For the ability of either or both parties does not belong to the essence of marriage. But if it was for time to come and conditional, then he or she who made the promise on this condition is free, and not bound in conscience to fulfill the promise, unless the condition stated beforehand is kept and performed.

Error of the quality of the person is when she who in the betrothal was taken to be a virgin is afterward found to be with child by another before they come together. By this error the covenant is made void and becomes an utter nullity. So the man cannot be compelled, once he truly and certainly knows it, to marry the woman, but may renounce her, unless both parties come to a new agreement, or have privately known each other by mutual consent. For first, God in express terms commanded the Jews that such a woman should be stoned to death. Deut 22:20: “If … no proof of the young woman’s virginity can be found” (that is, of the young woman given as a wife), v. 21: “she shall be brought to the door of her father’s house, and there the men of her city will stone her to death. For she has committed an outrage in Israel by being promiscuous in her father’s house.” Therefore it was not the will of God that she should be kept as a wife, but utterly rejected and forsaken. Again, this was so usual a practice in Israel, by God’s commandment, that godly and righteous men, on discovering this error, would not in conscience be persuaded to marry those to whom they had been betrothed. Matt 1:18, 19: “Because Joseph her husband was a righteous man and was unwilling to disgrace her publicly, he resolved to divorce her quietly” (he had found, before Mary and he came together, that she was with child).

III. Case. What are we to think of the betrothal of those who are raving or insane?

Answer. We must distinguish between these diseases. For madness is either perpetual, or by fits only, with intervals between.

If it is perpetual, the case is clear: whether only one of the parties is insane, or both, the contract made between them is altogether unprofitable and vain. For such persons do not know what they are doing when they make a promise. And the consent that passes between them cannot be free, full, and perfect, but must necessarily be hindered and impaired by the heat and violence of their disease.

Now although perpetual madness is a just impediment to marriage, and a sufficient cause to dissolve a contract, yet it is fitting that a suitable space of time be agreed on, in which all means may be used to cure this disease. The purpose is that God’s will concerning their recovery may be more plainly known, and that both the parties themselves and their families may testify to the world that they have had a careful regard for the contract made before.

Again, if it is not continual but by46 fits, so that they have some good days and quiet intervals, the case is different. For the contract will be ratified and stand in force, provided that it was plainly known that the said parties were both in their right minds before they pledged their troth to each other, and that they themselves are willing afterward to confirm the promise they made before by renewing their consent.

Consent of the parents is that act by which they give their word and promise to bestow their children in marriage, and, as to the right of it, do in fact bestow them at once.

Therefore private contracts made without the free and lawful consent of parents are not only unprofitable and unlawful, but even by the law of God utter nullities. Reasons. I. They are contrary to the express will and commandment of God. Exod 20: “Honor your father and mother.” II. They are flatly against natural equity, which teaches that he who has neither power nor right over himself cannot bind himself by promise to another. Now children do not have power over themselves,47 but are under the government and at the disposal of their parents. Therefore the covenants they make are not made and appointed by God; and those which God does not make are, in deed and truth, none at all.

7. Of Rejection, or Refusal of the Contract

Contrary to a complete and lawful contract48 is rejection, by which the contract is dissolved, or broken off.

A lawful contract is dissolved when some great and heinous fault follows immediately upon it in either of the betrothed parties. And from this arise various cases to be set down and resolved.

The first is this. What is to be done when some disease comes upon one of the parties immediately after the contract is made?

Answer. Those diseases that take away the use of the body, and altogether disable the party from performing the promise made with respect to marriage duties, are very just impediments to marriage, and so break off the contract. Of this sort are incurable palsies, frigidity, and the like, of which I have spoken before.

Nevertheless, a covenant once made is not to be renounced hastily, for fear of giving offense. And therefore some longer respite is to be taken from the time of the contract, in which they are to wait in expectation of recovery, before the said diseases are publicly and solemnly declared incurable, and so the covenant made is declared void.

Now, if the disease does not take away the use of the body for the present, and yet in time proves incurably contagious, and so loathsome that the one may justly fear to keep company and live with the other, as happens when one is infected with leprosy, then the contract is to be utterly dissolved, as if God himself had commanded it, though the promise was made before, and though the parties themselves should be unwilling. God has ordained matrimony to help, not to hurt, either the persons themselves or others. Where, therefore, there are such diseases as may infect, hurt, or destroy others, there God has, as it were, testified from heaven that the act done does not please him, and that it ought at once to be made void.

The contract being once dissolved in this way, the sounder party will be at liberty to marry again. But the diseased party is, by the magistrate’s authority, to be forbidden union with any other by way of marriage, and commanded to lead his life where he may fittingly live apart from company, for fear of infection. And for his own part he is also to seek from God, by prayer in faith, the gift of self-control. For it is certain that he to whom God has denied the power of using marriage with a good conscience is by that very fact called to self-control and single life.

But suppose the disease is not contagious, yet is either incurable or so foul that either of the betrothed has just cause to be afraid of the other’s company. Then both are to be advised not to claim their right, but willingly to surrender it to each other by mutual consent, so that they may be free again, and not bound by any former promise to live together as man and wife. For they have no hope of living together with comfort and contentment while they remain so.

Upon this advice, given by their lawful pastor or someone in his stead, if they both agree, or at least one of them desires to be at liberty, the betrothal is to be broken off at once. But if neither will consent to a separation, but they would rather proceed as they have begun, and in all probability the one has no just cause to hold the other in suspicion in respect of contagion, they are not to be hindered from completing their marriage.

Furthermore, one of them may have a disease that is continual, without intermission, and yet curable; or some other misfortune may come upon either of them after the sure-making, by which they become lame, deaf, or mute, etc. Yet this is not a sufficient cause to move them to renounce and dissolve the contract.

A second case. What if it happens that after the contract is finished, one of the betrothed persons is absent from the other for a long time, so that the absence is prejudicial to the marriage that should follow on the contract?

Answer. Inquiry must be made whether this absence is voluntary, or against the will of the party.

Suppose it is voluntary. For example, the man, on an honorable and just cause, the woman also knowing of it, goes overseas; and having been admonished of his duty beforehand, he nevertheless stays a whole year or more and will not return, but willfully absents himself further. Then it may be lawful for the woman to ask the public magistrate to dissolve the covenant made, and so to marry another man, unless the former man, to whom she was contracted, is heard of. If he is, then it will be lawful for him to plead for himself; and if he offers no just cause for his refusal, he will be compelled by the magistrate’s authority to stand by his promise and take the woman as his wife. And the same course is to be taken in the willful absence of the woman after she is contracted.

Again, if the man or the woman absents himself or herself and departs with an evil mind, and with the purpose of deceiving the other, then means must be used to have the party admonished of his or her duty. When that has been done, or at least attempted, and the offending party still will not appear, if the other who is present, certainly knowing his or her own lack of self-control, appeals to the magistrate, then after public and solemn notice is given the contract may be broken.

But on the other hand, either of them may be absent against his will, intending no fraud or deceit, but forcibly detained by captivity, imprisonment, sickness, force, banishment, deportation, or the like. Then the party present, if desirous of completing the marriage, ought either to make efforts to reach him and wait for his return, or to have certain notice of his death, before she promises herself to anyone else, or has to do with any other by way of marriage.

A third case. What if after the contract one of the parties becomes raving or mad?

Answer. If the disease is continual, without intermission, then in all equity and likelihood the betrothal is to be dissolved, unless both parties, after knowing and experiencing the disease, have known one another. Yet in this and all such cases it is fitting that all good means be tried and used, and sufficient time be given, for restoring the diseased to their former good condition, and for completing the marriage lawfully begun, as before.

48. Repudium.

8. Of Marriage

Marriage is that by which the union begun in the contract is solemnly made known and brought to perfection. Marriage is completed by three sorts of actions: one of the parents of the bride and bridegroom, the second of the minister in public, the third of the persons joined together.

The action of the parents is, on the wedding day, to bring the bride and deliver her to the bridegroom, so that the two may actually become man and wife, and perform all matrimonial duties to each other.

But suppose the marriage is completed in some other manner, so that the parents, on sound judgment and deliberation, deny their full and free consent, either in express words or tacitly and by silence, and that on just and lawful cause. There, though it may stand in the civil courts of men, and the children born in it be legitimate before men, yet in truth before God it is of no force, but an utter nullity.

And because this doctrine concerning the consent of parents in these cases is of great use, and does much to support and maintain families, I will first explain what it truly means, and then prove it by reasons.

Under the name of parents are included: First, the father and mother. Secondly, all guardians who have the particular and sole charge of wards, or of others under the years of discretion. Thirdly, all who are kindred by blood and stand in the place of parents to children, such as the uncle on the father’s side, the uncle on the mother’s side, and the like.

Now as to the consent of parents, that is, of father and mother, I hold it to be required of necessity for marriage. For the authority of parents must not be resisted or violated. As for guardians, and those who have the place of parents, their consent is not required of necessity, but49 at least of decency. For the power and authority of the parent, though it is not taken away, is yet lessened when it is either transferred to another person, or rests in part in the child already bestowed.

Secondly, by parents’ consent I mean that which they give, not rashly, unadvisedly, or foolishly, but from good and wise consideration, and on a true and sound judgment of the business in hand. For otherwise, as far as lies in them, they make the marriage void and of no effect. And they are thought to judge the matter rightly when they are able to give a just cause for giving or denying their consent. For example, if a father refuses to bestow his daughter Julia on Sempronius because he knows him to be an Arian, a Pelagian, or any other sort of heretic, he withholds his consent on a good ground, and what he does, he does from judgment.

Yet I add further that where the parents dissent and can give no reasonable cause for it, the marriage completed without their consent ought to be confirmed and ratified by the authority of the magistrate, who is Pater patriae [the father of the country]. And this seems to be the most equitable course, both to avoid greater scandals, and to prevent the wrong that might otherwise be done in some particular case, as to a woman who has been deflowered and rejected.

Thirdly, consent of parents is either expressed or implied: expressed when it is given in words, implied when it is given by silence. For it is most equitable and impartial to think that those parents give consent who do not expressly deny it in words.

Fourthly, children are either subject to the authority of their parents in the family, or at their own liberty and out of their parents’ subjection. Those who are at liberty are not necessarily tied to subjection in respect of marriage; but the others, being still of the family and under their parents’ jurisdiction, are bound to be ordered by their parents in bestowing themselves.

This, briefly, is the meaning of the question in hand. Now, to prove this point, I will propose three sorts of arguments: some drawn from the law of God, some from the light of nature, and some from the judgment of the ancient Church.

For the first sort. According to the law of God, marriage is not only a civil and political union but also a divine and spiritual one, whose author and ordainer, for a special cause, was God himself. Our Savior Christ witnesses this when he says, “What God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matt 19:6). Therefore, so that marriages may be soundly ratified and confirmed, the authority and power of God himself must necessarily be brought in.

If it is asked, How does God, who is in heaven, bring and join together man and wife on earth?

I answer that he does it not directly by himself, as he brought Eve to Adam, but in and by some solemn and lawful means. And this means is the great and ancient power and prerogative of parents. And the law of God has given them this power, not in civil contracts and agreements alone, but even in the beginning and completing of marriages. Deut 7:3: “Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons.” Jer 29:6: “Take wives for your+ sons and give your+ daughters in marriage, so that they too may have sons and daughters.” 1 Cor 7:36: “But if anyone thinks he is acting improperly toward his virgin daughter, if she is past the flower of her age and need so requires, let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married.”

Hence it was that Abraham, by right of this authority, gave orders what wife his servant should provide for his son: “You will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites … but will go to my country and my kindred to take a wife for my son Isaac” (Gen 24:3, 4). Samson, though he was inflamed with love for the woman in Timnah, whom he saw to be beautiful in his eyes, yet did not dare take her as his wife until she was given him by his parents (Judg 14). It was an express law of God that “if a man seduces a virgin who is not pledged in marriage and sleeps with her, he must pay the full dowry for her to be his wife.” But how? Note in what manner the Holy Spirit proceeds: “If her father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the man still must pay an amount comparable to the bridal price of a virgin” (Exod 22:16, 17; Deut 22:28, 29). In this text Moses plainly teaches that the consent of the two parties is not sufficient, no, not even though they have had union together, unless they also have the free consent of their parents. In like manner it was ordained by God, Num 30:3, 4, 5, that “if a woman in her father’s house … makes a vow to the Lord … and her father hears about her vow … but says nothing to her,” that is, approves her vow by passing it over, “then all the vows … shall stand. But if her father prohibits her,” that is, gives no approval or consent to the vow made, “then none of the vows … shall stand. The Lord will absolve her because her father has not consented.” Now if the vow of children made to God, and pertaining to his worship, cannot be ratified without the parents’ approval, how much less force will any private contract or marriage have without their allowance?

The second argument is taken from the light of nature, and it is drawn by analogy in this way. A son secretly alienates and sells away his father’s lands, either in whole or in part. The question is whether this alienation is good in law or not. Answer. No. And why? Because the land did not belong to the son, but was part of his father’s property. In like manner, a son alienates himself and is betrothed to a woman, to marry her without his parents’ knowledge. Is this act of the son warrantable and sound? By no means. For the son, in respect of his body, is part of the father’s goods, and must not be alienated from him without his consent. We find a notable reason for this in Job 1. For when God had given Satan power to destroy and spoil all Job’s goods and whatever he had, the devil touched not only Job’s wealth but his children also, as a part of his property. In this respect the Jews were permitted by God to sell their children (Exod 21:7).

Again, for marriage to be accomplished, there must be a mutual giving between the two betrothed. And what is it that is mutually given? Surely their persons, or rather their bodies, to each other; for so Paul says, 1 Cor 7:2: “each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.” But by whom is this giving to be made? By sons and daughters who are in the family, under the jurisdiction of their parents? It cannot be. For nature herself takes it for granted that he who is not at his own liberty cannot consent to the giving of himself. The giving therefore remains in the right of the parent, inasmuch as the will and consent of the child ought to depend on the will and consent of him to whom God has given power and authority in this matter.

In the third place, let the judgment of the ancient Church be observed. Ambrose, in his first book on the patriarch Abraham, ch. 9, requires this consent in marriages, and says it is so just and agreeable to nature that even the poets acknowledged it. For this purpose he recites two verses from the Greek poet Euripides, in his tragedy called Andromache. There, when Orestes desired to marry Hermione, she gives him this answer: that the matter of her marriage depended wholly on the pleasure and authority of her father, and was not in her own power or liberty. Innocent, who was both a pope and a martyr, in his decretal epistles so strictly requires the consent of parents50 that “where it is wanting, he concludes the marriage to be void.” In the Council of Lateran it was decreed that clandestine contracts and “secret marriages, made and undertaken between party and party, should be held as unlawful as marriages in those degrees of consanguinity and affinity which are forbidden by God.” Tertullian says51 that “in this world the son cannot52 rightly and lawfully marry without the allowance of his father.” Basil, in an epistle to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, affirms “that marriages which are made without those who have power over the parties are fornications; and therefore that those who are joined together in marriage while their parents or masters live are in no way free from the charge of sin until they have approval from them; for then marriage is ratified and confirmed, when they have given their allowance to it.”

The second action in completing marriage is the action of the minister. And that is the blessing or sanctification of it: a solemn work by which the minister, pronouncing the contracted parties to be man and wife before the whole congregation, commends them and their state to God by solemn prayer.

This solemn sanctification is grounded on the practice of God himself, who, having given Eve to Adam, blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Gen 2:22; 1:28). For what God then gave, the minister, standing in his place, now prays may be given to the man and wife. Indeed, it agrees with the general rule of the apostle, “Everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner” (1 Cor 14:40).

Now that this action is to be approved and used in the Church appears from these reasons.

  1. Marriage, as it is a public action, so it is in a sense a spiritual and divine ordinance, and in this it differs from the contract. For the contract, being merely civil, as it stands by the consent of men, so by the same consent it may be broken and dissolved; but with marriage it is otherwise.
  2. Marriage is the seedbed of the Church and commonwealth.
  3. It was the practice of the early Church. Tertullian, speaking of the marriage of Christians with Christians,53 acknowledges that he is not able sufficiently to declare the happiness “of that union which is made by the Church, consecrated by prayers and54 solemn service, witnessed by the angels, and ratified by God himself.” Nicephorus reports of one Synesius, who declared that “God and the laws, and the holy hand of Theophilus, had given him a wife.” Ambrose says “that marriage ought to be sanctified with the veil with which the priest used to cover the bride and the bridegroom in the public congregation, and with his blessing.”

The third and last action belonging to the completing of this state is that of the parties themselves, by which the bride is brought, in a decent and modest manner, to the house and home of the bridegroom. It is the law of this state, published by God himself in Paradise, that the man, even in respect of where he dwells, must “leave his father and mother and be united to his wife” (Gen 2:24).

Here the question is raised whether marriage is to be solemnized with mirth and feasting. Answer. I. It is lawful and warrantable to use feasting and mirth at marriages, because these are things neither commanded nor forbidden, and we have examples of them in the Scriptures. Laban made a feast at the wedding of Jacob and Rachel, and invited all the men of the place to it (Gen 29:22). Christ himself approved the gathering of people at the marriage at Cana in Galilee, both by his presence and by that honorable gift of six water jars of the best wine (John 2:2, 7, 8). II. It is not only lawful, but fitting and proper to be done, if there is ability, according to the commendable custom of the place and country where men live, provided that in its use these cautions are observed. First, that in mirth and merrymaking care be taken that nothing is done that is dishonorable, profane, or of ill report. Phil 4:8: “Whatever is honorable, … whatever is pure, … whatever is of good report … think on these things.” Secondly, that joy in them be mixed and tempered with the fear of God, without which laughter and rejoicing is sheer madness (Eccl 2:2). Thirdly, that it be done with a moderate and sober use of food and drink, without revelry and excess. So we read that at the great feast of Ahasuerus it was appointed by the king himself that they should drink in an orderly way, and none might compel another to drink more than he thought fitting (Esth 1:8). And where weddings are kept contrary to these directions, they are not feasts celebrated to God, but to the devil; which may also be said of all other festive gatherings.

And so much for the point of marriage. In it this is to be remembered as a conclusion: that where there is in general a nullity in the contract, or a separation following on it, there is also a nullity in regard to the completing of marriage.

9. Of the Duties of Married Persons

Thus far we have proceeded in the doctrine of marriage; and now we come to the duties which married persons are to perform to each other.

These are chiefly two: cohabitation and communion.

Cohabitation is their quiet and comforting dwelling together in one place, for the better performance of mutual duties. 1 Cor 7:10: “To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband.” v. 12: “To the rest I say this (I, not the Lord): If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not leave her.” v. 13: “And if a woman has an unbelieving husband and he is willing to live with her, she must not leave him.” 1 Pet 3:7: “Husbands, in the same way, live with your+ wives with consideration, giving honor to the woman as the weaker vessel and as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your+ prayers will not be hindered.”

This duty must be kept especially in the first year of marriage. Deut 24:5: “If a man is newly married, he must not be sent to war or be pressed into any duty. For one year he is free to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married.” And the ground of this commandment, no doubt, is that they might learn to know one another’s dispositions, and might form a settled affection for one another, which afterward could not be changed on any occasion.

Yet they may be absent from each other in two cases. First, by mutual consent for a time, to carry out some business that the family requires. Prov 7:19: “For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey … and will not return till the moon is full.” Secondly, such absence is allowed when some great and weighty affairs, either in the Church or the commonwealth, are in hand. 2 Sam 11:9, 10: “But Uriah slept at the door of the palace with all his master’s servants; he did not go down to his house.” v. 11: Uriah answered David, “The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in tents, and my master Joab and his soldiers are camped in the open field. How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!”

From this arises a question: What if, after the marriage is completed, a contagious disease comes upon one of the parties that cannot be cured, but is so loathsome that the other, healthy party cannot endure living together at all?

Answer. Both the marriage itself and the duty of dwelling together ought to continue firm and sure notwithstanding. Yet the sound party neither may nor ought, in good conscience, to desire union with the other by which he or she may bring infection upon themselves, and so hurt their children and endanger the commonwealth.

But if either of the parties does not have the gift of self-control and cannot abstain, they must seek it from God in earnest prayer, and he will give it to them.

For God has called a man or woman to self-control where they are necessarily hindered from the use of the ordinary and lawful remedy of the contract.

The contrary of cohabitation is desertion.

Desertion is when one of the married couple, from a willful and obstinate mind, and on his or her own initiative, departs from the other without a just and necessary cause.

On this point various cases are explained.

I. Case. Suppose that a husband who is an unbeliever, or a heretic in the fundamentals, of his own accord and out of hatred of the true religion, completely forsakes his believing wife and refuses to live with her any longer. What is to be done?

Answer. All good means must first be used to bring the infected party to repentance. And when none succeed, but the case remains desperate, then the marriage is dissolved on his part, and the believing wife is free to marry another. So says the apostle, 1 Cor 7:15: “But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called us to live in peace.” In these words observe a twofold reason. I. He who is at liberty may marry another. Now the believing party who is forsaken is at liberty, because he is not bound in such cases. Therefore he may marry another. II. God has called us to peace, says Paul; and this peace cannot be kept if the forsaken believing party cannot keep self-control unless he marries. Ambrose on the place says55 “that marriage cannot stand firm which is separated from the worship and service of God; and therefore it is no sin in the party who is forsaken for God’s cause to be married to another; and the unbeliever who departs sins both against God and against the law of wedlock, because he refuses to remain in that state on account of religion. Therefore he breaks the covenant of marriage, and the other is not bound in this case to keep faith with him.” Lombard, the Master of the Sentences,56 says “that the believing party in this case is not bound to follow the unbeliever when he departs, but while he lives may marry another.” Augustine57 affirms “that even the wife who is joined to her husband in lawful union, if she will not abide with her Christian husband because he is a Christian, may be forsaken and left without sin.” And it is far better that the covenant which man and wife have made with each other should be dissolved than the covenant which man has made with God. The people of Israel, being in affliction, were compelled to break the former, made with foreign women, so that they might keep the latter (Ezra 10:11, 19).

It is alleged that the unbelieving party may perhaps repent, and then to make a dissolution is in vain. But I say that it is just as likely that he will never repent, and therefore there is cause for the knot to be dissolved.

Again, some say that it is then lawful to make a divorce outside the case of adultery. Answer. The believing party who is forsaken is not the cause of the divorce, but suffers the separation wrongfully made by the unbeliever. And Christ, where he mentions the case of adultery (Matt 19), speaks of an equal marriage, whereas Paul speaks of an unequal one.

II. Case. What if a desertion happens between two married persons who are both believers?

Answer. The faulty person, who is the cause of this desertion, is to be compelled by the course of civil and ecclesiastical censure to perform his or her duty. If upon this proceeding he remains obstinate and perverse in will, the other must wait in patience and earnest prayer to God, until his mind may be changed and he is made to relent by the order of the magistrate. But if one of them, through a just occasion of fear, is compelled to depart from the other and cannot return without evident danger of life, in this case the one who departed is not bound to return; but the delinquent party is to remain alone until he or she is instructed and made willing to do his or her duty. And in the meantime the innocent party must be resolved that God has called him or her to single life.

Again, suppose that one is resolutely unwilling to live with the other, and on that account flees without any fault of the other. If the matter, after a long time, is sufficiently known beforehand, and all possible means have been used to reclaim the guilty person; and if, when called, he does not appear in person before the judge to give a reason for his act: then, after public and solemn declaration has been made, the minister may, on such desertion, pronounce the marriage dissolved. For he who out of malice flees from his mate is to be held on the same footing as an unbeliever who departs out of hatred of religion and the service of God (1 Tim 5:8).

However, if the place to which he has fled is unknown, and on his flight some fault is found in the plaintiff, she is not to be heard, or set at liberty, by the judge in this case, though she pleads lack of the gift of self-control.

But suppose he who fled comes back unexpectedly and claims his spouse. Then, if the former course has not been taken, nor judgment given against him, they may be reconciled and come together again. If it has, and matters are concluded, he is not to be heard on his return, but rather to be severely punished.

Like desertion is the malicious and spiteful dealing of married persons with one another.

Malicious dealing is when, living together, they demand intolerable conditions of each other; and when the one does not regard or relieve the other, being in danger or extremity, as is fitting. For this is as much as to betray one another’s fortunes and life to their utter enemies.

Here it may be asked what a believer should do who is in certain and imminent danger, either of loss of life or of breach of conscience, if they both remain together.

Answer. I. This certain danger has its origin either from a stranger or from one of the parties. If from a stranger, then the husband either takes on himself the defense of his believing wife, or he does not. If he does, then she ought to remain with him. If not, she may depart and provide for her own safety. II. Again, if the husband threatens harm, the believing wife may flee in this case; and it is all one as if the unbelieving man departed. For to depart from someone and to drive someone away by threats are equivalent.

Nor should it seem strange to anyone that the believer is allowed to depart in such a case. For a husband who is a Christian is married in two ways: first to Christ, and secondly to his wife. The former marriage is made in baptism, and is a holier union than the latter. Therefore, when these two cannot stand together, but one of them must necessarily be dissolved, the latter must be left rather than the former. Again, if the believer remained with the unbeliever, she might perhaps at times be pressed, in a case of danger, through infirmity, to deny Christ and make shipwreck of faith and good conscience, which may in no way be done by either party. And therefore separation is to be made in this society, rather than that the union with Christ should not stand firm and continue.

It is alleged that if this is so, then the believing wife forsakes the unbelieving husband, which she must not do.

Answer. She does not forsake him finally, but leaves him for a time. Again, the desertion is not made by the person who gives way for the time, but by him in whom the cause of the desertion lies; just as he is not to be called a schismatic who separates himself, but he in whom the cause of the schism lies.

Again, it is objected that he who flees leaves his calling, and every man must remain in his calling, according to the rule of the apostle (1 Cor 7:20).

Answer. There is a double calling: the general, which consists in the worship of God; the particular, as the calling of marriage or of single life. When these two callings cannot stand together, the latter must give way to the former. Luke 14:26: “If anyone comes to Me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be My disciple.”

III. Case. When the husband is perpetually absent from the wife, what is to be done?

Answer. If he is absent because he is in captivity, or out of malice, or fear, or any such cause, the wife must wait in expectation of his return until she has notice of his death, either by sufficient testimony or by evident likelihoods. Now, in the lack of testimonies and conjectures in this matter, if the forsaken party cannot determine with certainty that the absence was made with an evil mind, some have thought that she ought to wait for his return for the space of four years; others five; some seven, some ten years. After that time she is free, and may marry another man. And if the party who was probably thought to be dead does perhaps return after a long time, the latter marriage, undertaken in necessary ignorance of such an event, may be dissolved; and it will not be imputed to either party, since it happened not by their fault, but only by accident.

Now if the question is of willful and deliberate absence, the same is to be determined concerning it as has been said before on the point of desertion.

55. Ambros. in 1 Cor 7:15.

56. Libr. 4. dist. 39.

57. Lib. de Fide & operib. cap. 16.

10. Of the Communion of Married Folks

The communion of man and wife is that duty by which they mutually and willingly share with each other both their persons and their goods, for their mutual help, need and comfort. Eph 5:28: “Husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.”

This duty consists chiefly in the performance of a special marital duty toward one another, and that not as a courtesy, but as a debt that is due. 1 Cor 7:3: “The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.”

The marriage duty each owes the other must be shown with a singular and entire affection toward one another, and that chiefly in three ways.

First, by the right and lawful use of their bodies, that is, of the marriage bed, which is indeed an essential duty of marriage.

The marriage bed means that solitary and secret fellowship that is between man and wife alone.

And it is a thing neither commanded nor forbidden in its own nature, neither good nor bad; and so Paul counts it among things neither commanded nor forbidden, 1 Cor 7:27: “Are you committed to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you free of commitment? Do not look for a wife.” For this reason the Church of Rome errs in two contrary ways. First, in that it makes marriage a sacrament, and so makes every action of it good in its own nature. Secondly, in that they forbid marriage to certain persons; and the reason of the prohibition may seem to be this, that they think this secret coming together of man and wife to be filthiness.58 This was the judgment of Siricius, that filthy pope of Rome. He determined that marriage was the uncleanness of the flesh, and to that end he abused the words of the apostle in Rom 8:8, affirming that those who are in the flesh, that is, in the state of matrimony, “cannot please God.” Yes, and after marriage was condemned by them, some began to detest and hate women,59 as Ephraim the Syrian did, of whom the church histories make mention. And the Council of Trent is of the same judgment.60 For in setting marriage against chastity, it plainly determines that there is no chastity in marriage.

This coming together of man and wife, although it is neither commanded nor forbidden, is yet made a holy and undefiled action by the holy use of it. Heb 13:4: “Marriage is honorable among all, and the marriage bed undefiled.” And it is sanctified by the word and prayer, as all other created things and ordinances of God are. 1 Tim 4:3: “… They will forbid marriage …” and vv. 4, 5: “… nothing … should be rejected, … because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.” In this place we should observe how the apostle applies the point of sanctification directly to marriage.

The word of God gives direction to married folks in two ways. First, by giving them warrant that they may lawfully do this action; for whatever is not done in faith is sin, and that faith must be grounded on God’s word. Secondly, by prescribing the right and holy manner of doing it.

The holy manner stands in these particulars.

First, that it be done in moderation. For even in wedlock, excess in lusts is no better than plain adultery before God.61 This is the judgment of the ancient church: that intemperance, that is, immoderate desire even between man and wife, is fornication.

Secondly, that it be used with a holy abstinence.

Abstinence from this secret fellowship must be kept in two cases.

First, while the woman has her monthly flow. Lev 18:19: “You must not approach a woman to uncover her nakedness during her menstrual period.” And it is made one of the marks of a good man that he does not lie with a woman in her period, Ezek 18:6.

Secondly, in the time of a solemn fast, when some grievous calamity is at hand. Then they are to give themselves (by mutual consent) to fasting and prayer, 1 Cor 7:5: “Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you+ may devote yourselves+ to fasting and prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you+ through your+ lack of self-control.” 2 Sam 11:11: “Uriah answered David, ‘The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in tents, and my master Joab and his soldiers are camped in the open field. How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!’” Zech 12:12: “The clan of the house of David will mourn apart, and their wives apart; the clan of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart,” and so on.

Next to the word, this action may be sanctified by prayer for a blessing on it. Children are the gift of God, and therefore married folks are not only to use the means but also to pray that they may have them, Ps 113:9: “He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children.” Ps 127:3: “Children are indeed a heritage from the Lord, and the fruit of the womb is His reward.” Examples of this are these: Gen 25:21: “Isaac prayed to the Lord on behalf of his wife, because she was barren. And the Lord heard his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived.” 1 Sam 1:26, 27: “‘Please, my lord,’ said Hannah, ‘as surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the Lord.’” v. 27: “I prayed for this boy, and the Lord has granted me what I asked of Him.”

Now the fruits that are reaped and enjoyed by this holy use of the marriage bed are three.

  1. The having of a blessed seed. Deut 28:1: “Now if you faithfully obey the voice of the Lord your God …,” “the fruit of your womb will be blessed, as well as the produce of your land.” This is also called “the seed of God,” being begotten in a holy manner, Mal 2:15: “Has not the Lord made them one, having a portion of the Spirit? And why one? Because He seeks a seed of God. So guard yourselves+ in your+ spirit, and do not break faith with the wife of your+ youth.”
  2. The preservation of the body in cleanness, so that it may be a fit temple for the Holy Spirit to dwell in, 1 Thess 4:3, 4: “For it is God’s will that you+ should be holy: … each of you+ must know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God.”
  3. The holy state of marriage is a living type of Christ and his church, and this communion of married persons is also a figure of the union that is between him and the faithful, Hos 2:19: “I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion. And I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you will know the Lord.” Eph 5:23: “For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior.”

Here some questions are to be resolved.

Case. I. May marriage be dissolved in the case of barrenness?

Answer. No. For barrenness is for the most part a hidden infirmity, and one that God has often cured, even when it seemed hopeless, as in Sarah. Again, the fruit of the womb is God’s blessing and depends wholly on him. Therefore the man who rejects his wife for lack of children, when he received her at the hands of God, does wrong even to God himself.

Case II. What if either of the married folks commits fornication, or any sin of the same kind greater than fornication, such as incest, sodomy, lying with beasts, or the like?

Answer. Adultery and fornication are most grievous and open crimes, which break the very bond and covenant of marriage, Prov 2:17. And therefore when the married persons certainly know of them, they are by no means to be winked at, but the magistrate is to be informed of them at once. However, if the innocent party is willing to receive the adulterer again because of his repentance, then, so that the innocent party may not seem to favor and maintain sin, and to be himself one who practices uncleanness, he is to go to the congregation and declare the whole matter to the minister, so that the minister may understand the guilty party’s repentance and desire of forgiveness.

And if the adulteress has conceived and is in labor, the husband, to avoid being charged with having a bastard for his heir, is to report the adulteress’s repentance to the church, or to make certain persons acquainted with it. This is not so that she may be punished for the deed, but so that they may take notice of a child conceived in adultery, whom he may afterward lawfully disown as none of his.

When the matter is known, the innocent party may seek a divorce. For adultery is such a sin as breaks off completely not only the use but the bond and covenant of marriage. Matt 19:9: “Now I tell you+ that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman, commits adultery.” And yet the same bond may be continued and grow up again by the good will and consent of the innocent party; and so they may be reconciled and still live together. 1 Sam 25:44: “But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.” 2 Sam 3:14: “Then David sent messengers to say to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, ‘Give me back my wife, Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred Philistine foreskins.’” The innocent may take the same course in like cases, especially on the repentance of the guilty person. But still every man must be left to his own conscience, and no one is to be compelled against his will to take back the other party, from whom he may justly be separated.

Now in seeking a divorce there is an equal right and power in both parties, so that the woman may seek it as well as the man, and he as well as she. The reason is that they are equally bound to each other and have the same right in one another’s body; provided always that the man is to maintain his superiority, and the woman to observe the modesty that befits her toward the man.

After the divorce is made, it will be lawful for the innocent party, if he does not have the gift of self-control, to marry again, on leave obtained from the church and the Christian magistrate.

But what then will become of the offending party?

Answer. If, because his conscience is in danger for lack of the remedy, any liberty of a second marriage is to be granted him by the church or the civil magistrate (as indeed here in England there is not), several restraints must be observed in this case.

First, no such liberty is to be granted so long as it remains uncertain whether they may be reconciled, especially while the innocent party lives single. Secondly, it must plainly appear that the offending party has earnestly repented of his sin before he can either be received into the church or admitted to a second marriage. Thirdly, this liberty is not to be granted him either at once or rashly, but only after frequent and serious admonition that he should rather give himself to mourning and lamentation, and still remain alone, than desire to enjoy again the benefit of that state which he has already so shamefully abused.

So much for the first way of performing the marriage duty.

The second way is by cherishing one another. Eph 5:29: “No one ever hated his own flesh, but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church.” This cherishing is the performing of any duties that tend to the preserving of each other’s life. For this reason they are freely to share with each other their goods, their counsel and their labors, for the good of themselves and their own.

The third way is by a holy kind of rejoicing and solacing themselves with each other, in a mutual showing of the signs and tokens of love and kindness. Prov 5:18: “May you rejoice in the wife of your youth.” v. 19: “A loving doe, a graceful fawn—may her breasts satisfy you always; may you be captivated by her love forever.” Song 1:2: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is more delightful than wine.” Gen 26:8: “When Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from the window and was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah. Abimelech sent for Isaac and said, ‘So she is really your wife!’” Isa 62:5: “For as a young man marries a young woman, so your sons will marry you; and as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.”

This rejoicing and delight is permitted more to the man than to the woman; and to them both, more in their young years than in their old age.

11. Of the Husband

Married folks are either husband or wife.

The husband is he who has authority over the wife. For this reason Scripture calls him “the guide of her youth” (Prov 2:17). And since the two of them are but one flesh, he is also the head over his wife.

The duties of the husband toward the wife are these:

I. To love her as himself: Eph 5:33: “Each one of you+ also must love his wife as he loves himself.” Gen 24:67: “And Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took Rebekah as his wife. And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death.” Note how the husband’s love for his wife eases his sorrow for the death of his mother.

He is to show this love in two things. First, in protecting her from danger, Gen 20:16: “And he said to Sarah, ‘See, I am giving your brother a thousand pieces of silver. He is a covering of the eyes for you before all who are with you; you are completely cleared.’” 1 Sam 30:5: “David’s two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel, had been taken captive.” v. 8: “David inquired of the Lord: ‘Should I pursue these raiders? Will I overtake them?’ ‘Pursue them,’ the Lord replied, ‘for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives.’” Secondly, in regarding her welfare as his own, and providing maintenance for her, both for his lifetime and, as far as he can, for the time to come after his death. Eph 5:28: “Husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.” v. 29: “No one ever hated his own flesh, but he nourishes … it,” and so on. Exod 21:10: “If he takes another wife, he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of his first wife.” Ruth 3:9: “‘Who are you?’ he asked. ‘I am your servant Ruth,’ she replied. ‘Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer.’”

II. To honor his wife: 1 Pet 3:7: “… giving honor to the woman …”

This honor stands in three things. First, in esteeming her as his companion, or yoke-fellow. For this reason the woman, when she was created, was not taken out of the man’s head, because she was not made to rule over him; nor out of his feet, because God did not make her subject to him as a servant; but out of his side, so that the man should take her as his mate. Secondly, in a wise and patient bearing or covering of her infirmities, such as anger, waywardness and the like, in respect of the weakness of her sex. 1 Pet 3:7: “… giving honor to the woman as the weaker vessel and as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your+ prayers will not be hindered.” Thirdly, by allowing himself at times to be admonished or advised by her. It was God’s commandment to Abraham concerning his wife Sarah: “Do not be distressed about the boy and your maidservant. Listen to everything that Sarah tells you, for through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (Gen 21:12). So Elkanah was willing to agree to his wife Hannah’s advice that she stay at home till the child was weaned, 1 Sam 1:23: “‘Do what you think is best,’ her husband Elkanah replied, ‘and stay here until you have weaned him. Only may the Lord confirm His word.’” For this reason the heathen philosopher said,62 “The master of the family exercises (after a sort) a tyrannical power over his servants, and a royal power over his children, because kings are fathers of their commonwealths; but toward his wife he exercises an aristocratic power, not according to his own will, but agreeable to the honor and dignity of the married state.” And so, he said, the husband ought not in modesty to claim the privilege of directing and advising his wife in all household matters, but in some to leave her to her own will and judgment.

Here the question is raised whether the husband may punish his wife.

Answer. Though the husband is the wife’s head, yet it seems that he has no power or liberty granted him in this respect. For we do not read in the Scriptures any precept or example to warrant such a use of his authority. He may reprove and admonish her in words only, if he sees her at fault. For so we read that Jacob rebuked his wife when she was impatient, and that even in anger, Gen 30:2: “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?” And Job rebuked his wife, Job 2:10: “You speak as a foolish woman speaks. … Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” But he must not chastise her, either with lashes or with blows. The reason is plain: wives are their husbands’ mates, and the two of them are one flesh. And no man hates, much less beats, his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, Eph 5:29. Again, it is God’s commandment that a man should not trespass against the wife of his youth, Mal 2:15. Chrysostom says,63 “It is the greatest reproach that can be for any man to beat his wife.” Plutarch, in the life of Cato the Censor, affirms that “he who strikes his wife” does the same “as if he should lay violent hands on the sacred images of the gods”; and this was counted a high degree of offense among the heathen.

It is alleged that husbands are commanded to love their wives as Christ loves his church; now Christ chastises his church with blows; and therefore the husband may do so to his wife. Answer. As Christ loves his church entirely, so he may also chastise it, because he is not only its husband but also its absolute Lord and King. But the husband is not so absolute over the wife.

But, it is said, his authority over the wife is in a certain sense civil, as is the authority of the magistrate over his people. Answer. It is not so. For the magistrate has the power of the sword in his hand, and by that power he inflicts punishment for offenses. But the husband can claim no such power for himself.64 Indeed, it is flatly forbidden in the civil law that he should scourge or strike his wife.

Nevertheless, if she grows to extremities and is desperately perverse, so that there is no hope of amendment, then the magistrate may be informed. To prevent scandals and to provide for public peace, the magistrate both ought and may assign to her necessary correction and punishment according to what she deserves. Now the husband who has so stubborn and contrary a wife must bear it, if it can be borne, as the portion of his cross laid on him by God. And in this case, if he is impatient, he may in some sort be pardoned and pitied, but he is not wholly to be excused.

63. In 1 Cor 11. Homil. 26.
