12. Of the Wife

The wife is the other married person, who, being subject to her husband, yields obedience to him.

The word of God mentions the subjection of the wife in various places. Rom 7:2: “A woman in subjection to a husband is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives.” Eph 5:24: “As the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything.” Col 3:18: “Wives, submit to your+ husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.” 1 Tim 2:12: “I do not permit a woman … to exercise authority over a man.” And it was a law God established immediately after the fall, Gen 3:16: “To the woman He said: ‘I will sharply increase … Your desire will be subject to your husband, and he will rule over you.’” Indeed, according to the civil law, the daughter, even when she is married, is65 in the power of her father, and not of her husband. But this is directly against the law of Moses, and goes against the law of nature, Lev 22:12, 13; Num 30:13.

Now the duties of the wife are chiefly two.

The first is to submit herself to her husband, and to acknowledge and reverence him as her head in all things. Gen 20:16: in the same way Abimelech said to Sarah, “See, your brother” (that is, your husband, whom you call your brother) “is a veil for your eyes before all who are with you.” As if he should say, Your husband is your head, and has power over you, and you ought to reverence him. For in ancient times the wife was covered with a veil in the presence of her husband, as a token of subjection to him. So Rebekah, at the sight of Isaac, took her veil “and covered herself” (Gen 24:65). 1 Cor 11:3: “The head of the woman is man.” Eph 5:22: “Wives, submit to your+ husbands as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church.” The reason for this is good. For the wife enjoys the privileges of her husband, and is graced by his honor and standing among men. His nobility makes her noble, though otherwise she is of low and humble rank; as, on the other hand, his lowliness and low degree cause her to be low and humble in rank, though she is noble and honorable by birth.

The second duty is to be obedient to her husband in all things; that is, to depend wholly on him, both in judgment and in will. For just as the church yields obedience to Christ her head, and yields herself to be commanded, governed and directed by him, so ought the woman to the man. So Sarah is said to have “obeyed Abraham,” and to have given him the terms of obedience: she “called him lord,” or sir (1 Pet 3:6). From this it follows that the woman is not to take the liberty of wandering and straying away from her own house without the man’s knowledge and consent. 2 Kgs 4:22: “And the woman called her husband and said, ‘Please send me one of the servants and one of the donkeys, that I may go quickly to the man of God and return.’” Again, it follows that she is to follow her husband when he moves or departs from place to place, unless he forsakes either her or Christ. To this purpose Paul says that he had the “right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles” (1 Cor 9:5). So Sarah went with Abraham into Egypt, Gen 12:11; and out of Egypt, Gen 13:1; and to Gerar, to sojourn there, Gen 20:1, 2, 3. So too the wives of Jacob departed with him from their father Laban, Gen 31:17.

Contrary to these duties are the sins of wives: to be proud; to be unwilling to bear the authority of their husbands; to scold and quarrel bitterly; to forsake their houses; and the like. Prov 27:15: “A constant dripping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike.” v. 16: “Restraining her is like holding back the wind or grasping oil with one’s right hand.” Exod 4:26: “When Zipporah said, ‘bridegroom of blood,’ she was referring to the circumcision.” It was the fault of the Levite’s concubine, Judg 19:2: “She was unfaithful to him and left him to return to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah,” and she was there four months. It was the sin of Queen Vashti, who “refused to come at the king’s command brought by his eunuchs. And the king became furious, and his anger burned within him” (Esth 1:12). Lastly, to be a cause of grief to their kindred. So the proud wives of Esau, the daughters of the Hittites, were a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah, Gen 26:35; 27:46.

65. In potestate patris.

13. Of the Parent

So far we have treated the first couple of which the family consists, namely married folks. Now the others follow, and they are of two sorts: either those by whom the family is increased and multiplied, or those who are helps to it.

Those by whom the family is enlarged are also of two sorts: parents and children.

Parents are those who have power and authority over children.

The duties of parents are chiefly two: one, to bring up their children; the other, to bestow them when they have brought them up.

As to the education or bringing up of children, the parents’ care must be both that they may live and also that they may live well, Eph 6:4.

As to the preserving of the child’s life, many duties are required of the parents, chiefly four. First, the mother is herself to nurse the infant and to wrap it in swaddling cloths. Paul commends it as a mark of a good wife that she nurses her own children, 1 Tim 5:10. So Sarah nursed Isaac, Gen 21:7. Hannah nursed Samuel, 1 Sam 1:22. David in all likelihood was nursed by his mother, Ps 22:9: “You made me secure at my mother’s breast.” And our Savior Christ was also nursed by Mary his mother, Luke 11:27, and swaddled, Luke 2:7. Now the reason for this is plain. God has given milk to women who bear children, and has so appointed that no food is more natural to the child than the mother’s milk. And nature itself teaches this in the course of other created things. The earth nourishes what it brings forth. The fruit the tree bears is fed by the sap that comes from its root. Yes, among the brute beasts, even those that are most savage, such as tigers, the mothers nurse the young they bring forth.

Yet in case of lack of health or ability, or any other just hindrance, the mother may in fairness be excused, and the child committed to a nurse. And so we read that Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel and afterward the wife of Isaac, had a nurse, Gen 24:59, whose name was Deborah, Gen 35:8. And Pharaoh’s daughter, in a case of necessity, committed Moses to be nursed by a Hebrew woman, whom she took to be not his mother but a stranger; and her deed was approved by God, Exod 2:7, 9.

The second duty of the parent is to provide food, drink and clothing for his child. Our Savior Christ says that parents, even by the light of nature, though they are evil, will not deny or withhold necessary food from their children. Matt 7:9, 10: “Which of you+, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?” And Paul says, “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim 5:8).

The third duty is, when God gives ability and means, to lay up something for the future maintenance of the child. 2 Cor 12:14: “… For children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.” Prov 19:14: “Houses and wealth are inherited from fathers.”

The fourth is to observe both the inclination and the natural gifts of body and mind that are in the child, and accordingly to place it in some honorable calling and course of life. Prov 20:11: “Even a child is known by his actions—whether his conduct is pure and upright.” In the church history66 written by Rufinus it is recorded that Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, saw from afar, in a place near the sea, a company of children playing together, and in their play imitating him in various ministerial actions. When he had watched them for a while, he perceived that they examined and baptized one another according to the solemn order used in the congregation. He made some of his clergy acquainted with this, and gave order that the children should be sent for and brought before him. Then he asked them what game they played, and in what manner they played with one another. At first the children, out of fear, denied what they had done; yet on further examination they confessed that they had made Athanasius (who afterward became bishop of that place) their bishop, and that he had instructed and baptized several of their company. Alexander further asked both Athanasius himself and those who were said to have been baptized what questions Athanasius had asked them, and what answers they had given. By their speeches he perceived that they had framed themselves, though in play, to the church’s proceedings in those actions. So, after conference with his clergy, he determined that those who had first been asked, and had answered fully according to the form used in that church, and had thereupon been baptized, should not be rebaptized. And as for Athanasius and the other children who had done the part of ministers in their kind, he sent for their parents and gave them a strict charge that they should be brought up in learning and religion, so that in time they might be fit for the public ministry. We read that the heathen took a like course to judge the inclination and aptness of their children.67 The Athenians made a law that before children were placed in any calling, they should first be brought into a public place where instruments belonging to all sorts of trades were laid out. And whatever kind of instrument any of them took most delight in, the child was thought to be most fit for the trade to which that instrument belonged, and was afterward set to it with good success.

Now the parents’ first and chief care must be for the church: that those of their children who have the readiest minds and are endowed with the best gifts be consecrated to God, and brought up in the study of the Scriptures, to serve afterward in the ministry of the church. So Hannah dedicated her son Samuel to God by vow, 1 Sam 1:11: “And she made a vow, pleading, ‘O Lord of Hosts, if only You will … give Your maidservant a son, then I will dedicate him to the Lord all the days of his life.’” And she did according to her vow, and the Lord blessed her son Samuel, who in time became a great prophet.

The next point of the education of children is to provide that they may live well and lead a godly life. To this end parents must do three things.

First, they are to take care that the child, as soon as may be after it is born, is admitted into the true church of God by baptism, and has a fit name given to it.

Secondly, they are to endeavor to sow the seeds of godliness and religion in the heart of the child as soon as it comes to the use of reason and understanding; and as it grows in years, care must be taken that it grows in knowledge and grace. To this end serves the vow and promise made in baptism, which parents are bound to call on the child to remember when it comes of age. It was the godly care of Timothy’s parents, 2 Tim 3:14: “But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them.” v. 15: “From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.” This was God’s commandment to the parents of his people, Deut 6:7: “These words I am commanding you … you shall teach diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home.” And v. 20: “In the future, when your son asks, ‘What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the Lord our God has commanded you+?’ then you are to tell him, ‘We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt …’” This was observed by the Israelites in the ages that followed: Ps 44:1: “We have heard with our ears, O God; our fathers have told us the work You did in their days, in the days of old.”

Thirdly, the first instruction of children in learning and religion must be so ordered that they may take it with delight. For this purpose they may at times be allowed to play in a moderate manner, and to refresh themselves in recreations fitting for their years. And if they do amiss in either, they are to be restrained by the bridle of discipline: first by reproof in words, and when that will not help, by the rod of correction. Zech 8:5: “And the streets of the city will be filled with boys and girls playing there.” Prov 29:15: “A rod of correction imparts wisdom, but a child left to himself disgraces his mother.” v. 17: “Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul.” Heb 12:9: “We have all had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them.”

Yet in this point two extremes are carefully to be avoided: that the parent be neither too severe nor too indulgent toward the child. Against severity Paul gives his rule, Eph 6:4: “Parents, do not provoke your+ children to wrath,” that is, by too much harshness in government. For leniency we have old Eli’s example, 1 Sam 2:23, 24: “‘Why are you+ doing these things?’ Eli said to his sons. ‘I hear about your+ wicked deeds from all these people. No, my sons …’” So much for education.

The second general duty of parents is the bestowing of their children. This bestowing is when parents, knowing their children to be fit for marriage and not to have the gift of self-control, use their best endeavor to provide matches for them in time, or at least advise them to it, by themselves or by their families: 1 Cor 7:36: “If anyone thinks he is acting improperly toward his virgin daughter, if she is past the flower of her age and need so requires, … they should get married.” v. 38: “He who gives her in marriage does well.” Jer 29:6: “Take wives … Take wives for your+ sons and give your+ daughters in marriage,” and so on. Gen 28:1: “So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him. ‘Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women,’ he commanded. ‘Go at once to Paddan-aram … and take a wife from among the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother.’” Judg 14:2, of Samson: “So he returned and told his father and mother, ‘I have seen a daughter of the Philistines in Timnah. Now give her to me as a wife.’”

This duty is nowadays carelessly neglected by parents, and its fruit is dangerous. For from this it comes about that their children often either commit whoredom or enter into wicked and ungodly marriages.

In the choice of a husband or wife, the parents ought to have greater regard for piety and wisdom than for beauty and riches, or any other outward blessings. Yet where they all meet together, the party so qualified is to be received all the more thankfully. On these grounds the priest or prince of Midian gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses, and Moses agreed to take her, Exod 2:19: “An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds. … He even drew water for us and watered the flock. … Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage.” Josh 15:16: “And Caleb said, ‘To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.’” Indeed, it is a sin to marry only for beauty, without consideration of the better things. So the old world sinned, when “the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose” (Gen 6:2). And so did Samson, who, only on the sight of the woman in Timnah, of the daughters of the Philistines, without further inquiry, desired that she might be given him as his wife, Judg 14:2.

Again, it is fitting that parents should deal moderately with their children in this case, and by no means undertake to force and compel them to marry this or that party. This was the just commendation of Rebekah’s parents: though they were idolaters, yet they had such regard for fairness that they first called her and asked her consent before they sent her away with Abraham’s servant to be married to Isaac, Gen 24:58. Now if the parents fail in their duty in this respect, the son or daughter may lawfully lay the matter first before their kinsfolk, and afterward (if need be) before the minister or magistrate, and seek redress by their means and direction.

66. Ruffin. Eccles. hist. lib. 1. c. 14.

67. Nazianz. epist. ad Eudoxam.

14. Of the Son

The son is he who is in subjection to his parents.

The duties a son is to perform to his parents are chiefly two.

First, to yield them obedience, whether they are his natural parents or otherwise, as his stepfather and stepmother, and that as long as he lives. Eph 6:1: “Children, obey your+ parents in the Lord, for this is right.” Luke 2:51: “Then He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them.” Exod 18:19: Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “Now listen to me; I will give you some advice, and may God be with you.” Ruth 3:5: Ruth said to Naomi her mother-in-law, “I will do everything you say.” Job 1:5: “And when the days of feasting were over, Job would send for his children to purify them.”

This obedience must show itself in two things.

First, in the choice of a lawful calling, in which the child is to be directed and appointed at the discretion of the parent.

Secondly, in marriage. For in that the parent is the chief agent and disposer of the child. Now his authority is not so great that the child is to be forced and compelled by him. Yet the reverent and dutiful respect which the child ought to bear toward him ought to be a strong inducement not to dissent from his advice, or reject it, without great and weighty cause. Indeed, the child must endeavor by every kind of dutiful conduct to overcome, or at least to soften, his parents’ severity in that matter.

Now for the daughters: they must yield obedience to their parents in all household labors, so that they may be skillful in household affairs. So the seven daughters of the priest of Midian accustomed themselves to draw water and fill the troughs “to water their father’s flock” (Exod 2:16). So Rebekah was seen to come out of her father’s house with her jar on her shoulder, and to go down with it to the well to fill it, and to give drink to her father’s camels (Gen 24:16, 17).

The second duty of the son is to repay his father’s love and care over him by relieving him in time of need, if God gives the ability, with food and clothing and other necessities. In this, children must deal with their parents as the brood of the stork is reported to deal with her, feeding her when she is old; and in doing so they do no more than what she did for them before. It is Paul’s counsel that children and grandchildren should repay the kindness of their kindred in the first place (1 Tim 5:4); and therefore of their parents, the head and foundation of their kindred. When Joseph was in prosperity and his father Jacob in need, he first gave him grain freely, and afterward sent for him to Egypt and provided for him there. So much so that the text says of him that he “provided his father and brothers and all his father’s household with food,” even as the mother puts food into the child’s mouth (Gen 47:12). When Naomi, Ruth’s mother-in-law, was of great age and her strength was spent, Ruth gathered grain in the harvest for the relief of them both. Indeed, when Boaz gave her food and drink, she kept back part of her meal and brought it home with her gleanings to refresh her mother-in-law (Ruth 2:14, 18).

The necessity of performing these duties is so great that if the son neglects them and does the contrary, by ill-treating his parent either in word or deed, he is worthy of death, even by Moses’ law. Exod 21:15: “Whoever strikes his father or mother must surely be put to death.”

The law of the firstborn among a man’s children, that he should have a greater portion of his father’s goods than any of the rest of his brothers, is perpetual. It admits no exception except in the case of notorious wickedness. Deut 21:17: “He must acknowledge the firstborn, the son of his unloved wife, by giving him a double portion of all that he has. For that son is the firstfruits of his father’s strength; the right of the firstborn belongs to him.” This was the law. Yet we read that Reuben lost this prerogative because of his incest, and Judah, the fourth son of Jacob, had the dignity of the firstborn. Gen 49:8: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you. … Your father’s sons shall bow down to you.”

In the Church of the Old Testament the privilege of the firstborn was threefold: the first of government and royalty, the second of priesthood, the third of the double portion. And it is probable that this was for the most part ceremonial, and was fulfilled and ended in Christ, who is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation” (Col 1:15).

Here two questions are put forward.

Question I. Is it lawful for the son to make a vow concerning either religion or civil life without the consent of the parent?

Answer. A vow so made has no force to bind the child, but by the law of nature and common equity it is to be made void. For it is a settled case that he who is not his own man (that is to say, not at his own liberty, but under the power of another) cannot bind himself. Again, the authority of the parent by the law of God is great. For it allows the father to make void the vow of the child concerning God’s worship (Num 30:5).

Question II. Is the consent of the parents to be required in the second marriages of their children?

Answer. 1. In ancient times it was provided, both by68 civil laws and also by imperial constitutions, that no widows, though made free by their former marriages, should make any contract again without the goodwill of their parents. 2. Consent in this case, though it is not absolutely necessary, is yet to be thought fit and proper. For children who are in some respects exempted from their parents’ authority still owe them the duty of honor, by God’s express commandment (Exod 20:12). And so they ought to show it by being directed and advised by them in some measure, even when they give themselves in marriage a second time. That is why69 later divines have held, on good ground, that the betrothals of widows, who have somewhat more liberty than a child married for the first time, cannot escape just blame if they are made without their parents’ knowledge, however much they may stand in force without it.

68. C. de Nuptijs. L. vidua, & L. in coniunctione.

69. Beza de repud. & diuort. sect. de sponsalibus absque consensu parentum factis.

15. Of the Master

Next to parents and children, by whom the family is increased, comes a second sort of couple, which are helps to it. And they are masters and servants.

The master is a member of the family who has power and bears rule over the servant. And his duty stands chiefly in three things.

First, to make a good choice of his servants. This is done when he looks first for those who fear God and are willing to serve him. Paul makes the service and fear of God the main ground of true obedience in servants (Eph 6:5, 6, 7; Col 3:22). It was the rule of David’s choice. Ps 101:6: “He who walks in the way of integrity shall serve me.” Abraham’s chief servant of his house was a man who feared God, as appears in that he made conscience of his oath (Gen 24:2, 3), and also prayed for success in the business he was sent about. Gen 24:12: “O Lord, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham.” Cornelius of Caesarea, the centurion of the Italian Regiment, had a soldier who attended on him daily and who feared God, and servants besides him, to whom he made known the heavenly vision he had seen (Acts 10:7).

Secondly, to assign them their labor, and not to require more of them than their strength will bear. The master is to rule over the servant in justice. And his command is unjust when it will not stand with the course of nature, with the ability of his servant, or with the word of God. Therefore he is to require of them labor in proportion to their strength, and to give them times of respite and rest. Lev 25:46: “But as for your+ brothers, the Israelites, no man may rule harshly over his brother.” 1 Pet 3:8: “Be … sympathetic, … be tenderhearted and humble.” And for the furthering of business it is fitting that the master be often present with the servants at their work. Prov 27:23: “Be sure to know the state of your flocks, and pay close attention to your herds.” The good matron “watches over the affairs of her household” (Prov 31:27).70 A man of Libya was asked what it was that might make a horse fat. He answered, “The master’s eye.”

Thirdly, to reward the diligence and pains of his servant, and that in three ways.

First, by giving him his due of food and drink at the present time. The good matron provides “food for her household and portions for her maidservants” (Prov 31:15).

Secondly, by paying him his wages at the end of his service. “The worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). “Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!” (Matt 25:21).

Here three caveats are to be observed. I. That the wages be in proportion to the work. II. That they be paid in due time, without delay. So the master of the vineyard, “when evening came,” called his servants together to “pay them their wages” (Matt 20:8). III. That the servant not be defrauded of any part of his due. For this is a crying sin. Deut 24:15: “You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, … Otherwise he may cry out to the Lord against you, and you will be guilty of sin.” Jas 5:4: “Look, the wages you+ withheld by fraud from the workmen who mowed your+ fields are crying out against you+. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.”

Thirdly, if the servant is sick during his time of service, the master’s care must be to procure his recovery by all possible means. Equity must be the rule in these cases, and masters are to give their servants “what is right and fair” (Col 4:1). Now the servant perhaps falls sick through his service and while in it. And his health brings not only profit to his master, but also encouragement to himself. The good centurion, when his servant was sick, took the best course to have him restored (Matt 8:6).

70. Arist. Oeconom. 7.

16. Of the Servant

The servant is a person in the family who is subject to his master.

The duty of a servant is to conduct himself faithfully and diligently in the affairs of his master, and to serve him as he would serve Christ, though the master be harsh and hard-hearted. Titus 2:9: “Servants are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative.” Eph 6:5: “Servants, obey your+ earthly masters with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you+ would obey Christ.” Col 3:22. So Jacob served Laban. Gen 31:38: “I have been with you for twenty years now. Your sheep and goats have not miscarried, nor have I eaten the rams of your flock,” etc.

On the other hand, the servant must take heed that he does not do his master’s business negligently, or for appearance’ sake, or with eye-service, as a man-pleaser; that when he is rebuked or reproved he does not answer back; and lastly, that he is trustworthy, and keeps his hands from pilfering and his heart from deceiving his master.

Servants are of two sorts: either free servants or bond-servants.

A free servant is one whom his master hires for wages to serve him. To him belongs the just payment of his wages. And if he offends, the master has authority to censure and punish him, provided that in doing so regard is had to his age, and the correction is used with moderation, as if he were his son.

A bond-servant is a servant bought for money, and is commonly called a slave. Concerning this sort a question is raised: may a Christian with a good conscience have and use a man as his slave?

Answer. The power and right of having bondmen, in those countries where it is established by positive laws, may stand with a good conscience, if it is used with moderation. Authority in this matter is moderate when these seven caveats are observed.

I. That the master does not have the power of life and death over his servant. For this takes away the lawful power of the magistrate, to whom alone the Lord has committed the sword of justice.

II. That he is not given liberty to use his servant at his own will and pleasure in all things. For this was not granted by the law of God to his own people. Exod 21:26: “If a man strikes and blinds the eye of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the eye. And if he knocks out the tooth of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the tooth.”

III. That the power is not enlarged to commanding things against piety or justice. For in these cases a man must obey God rather than man (Acts 4:19).

IV. That masters do not take liberty to separate those of their servants who are married from one another, or those who are parents from their children. For God himself has made these societies and joined such persons together, and therefore man must not separate them.

V. That masters do not take liberty to hand over their servants to ungodly and unbelieving masters. For that is an unkind and cruel liberty, and may be an evident occasion of making the servant fall away from religion and renounce the true God.

VI. That they do not bind them to perpetual slavery and never set them free. Exod 21:5: “But if the servant declares, ‘I love my master and my wife and children; I do not want to go free.’”

VII. That the servitude is not procured and kept by force. For it is a more grievous crime to rob a man of his liberty than of his riches.

Now that this same power, limited by these cautions, is lawful and warranted in conscience appears by these reasons.

I. God has ordained and allowed it, even by warrant of his own law. The posterity of Ham was cursed by Noah and condemned to slavery. Gen 9:25: “And he said, ‘Cursed be Canaan! A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.’” So were the Gibeonites by Joshua. Josh 9:23: “Now therefore you+ are under a curse and will perpetually serve as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of my God.” So was the thief. Exod 22:3: “A thief must make full restitution; if he has nothing, he himself shall be sold for his theft.” Again, those who are overcome in war may be held captive. It is lawful for the conqueror to kill them, and therefore to make them slaves. And if, being taken, they are saved from death, they owe all that they have to those by whom they are saved.

II. The law of God gave liberty to any man who wished to sell himself to another. Lev 25:45: “You+ may also purchase them from the foreigners residing among you+ or their clans living among you+ who are born in your+ land. These may become your+ property.” Deut 15:12: “If a fellow Hebrew, a man or a woman, sells himself to you and serves you six years, then in the seventh year you must set him free.” And v. 17: “Then take an awl and pierce it through his ear into the door, and he will become your servant for life.”

III. The man who is ransomed from his enemy is bound to serve as a slave in return, out of thankfulness.

IV. The examples of the godly in the Scriptures. Abraham had servants whom he bought with silver. Gen 17:12: “Generation after generation, every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old, including those born in your household and those purchased from a foreigner—even those who are not your offspring.” Gen 24:35: “The Lord has greatly blessed my master … He has given him sheep and cattle, silver and gold, menservants and maidservants, camels and donkeys.”

V. The apostles do not disapprove of such servants. They command them, being servants and called to profess Christianity in that state, not to change it, but to remain in their calling. 1 Cor 7:21: “Were you a servant when you were called? Do not let it concern you.”

It is alleged that such servitude is against the law of nature. Answer. It is indeed against the law of nature in its integrity, as it was before the fall; but it is not against the law of corrupted nature since the fall.

But Christ has purchased liberty for believers (Col 3:11). Answer. Only a spiritual liberty in this life, and a bodily liberty only in the life to come. For in regard of faith and the inner man the servant is equal to his master, because in Christ Jesus there is neither master nor servant, bond nor free. Yet in regard of the outward man and civil order among men, the master is above the servant, and the servant is, and must be, subject to the master.71 Nevertheless, where this kind of servitude is abolished, it is not to be received or admitted again among Christians, especially considering that it is a far milder and more moderate course to have hired servants.

If it is said again that the heathen philosopher holds servitude to be natural, so that some are bond by birth and others free, I answer: servitude does not proceed from nature,72 but has its origin from the laws of nations, and is a consequence of the fall. For all men by nature are equally and alike free, none more or less than others.

71. Theodor. Orat. 8.

72. Aristot. polit. lib. 1.

17. Of the Master of the Family or Goodman of the House

So much for the various and distinct combinations or couples belonging to the state of household government. From these arise two persons of a mixed or compound nature and condition, commonly called the master and the mistress of the house.

The master of the family, or goodman of the house, is a person in whom rests the private and particular government of the whole household. He does not come to it by election, as happens in other states, but by the ordinance of God, settled even in the order of nature. The husband indeed naturally bears rule over the wife, parents over their children, masters over their servants. But the person who by the providence of God has the place of a husband, a father and a master in his house, also has by the light of nature the chief place and sovereignty in it. He is the paterfamilias, the father and chief head of the family. To him therefore the true right and power over all household matters rightfully belongs. The duties of the master of the family are chiefly five.

I. To bear the chief part, and to be the principal agent, director and furtherer of the worship of God within his family. Josh 24:15: “As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.” And this he does partly by praying for and with his household, and partly by instructing them in the holy Scriptures and in the grounds of religion, so that they may grow in knowledge and reap benefit from the public ministry. This is how God commanded the men of Israel to walk in their families. Deut 6:7: “And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home … when you lie down and when you get up.” Again, v. 20: “When your son asks, ‘What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the Lord our God has commanded you+?’ then you are to tell him, ‘We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.’” God gave this testimony of Abraham before the law was given. Gen 18:19: “For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord.” And this household of Abraham was very large. For the Holy Spirit says long before that he had “318 trained men73 born in his household” (Gen 14:14). It was probably the course of Solomon, which he had learned from his father David and given as a rule to all masters of families. Prov 4:1: “Listen, my sons, to a father’s instruction; pay attention and gain understanding. … When I was a son to my father, tender and the only child of my mother, he taught me and said, ‘Let your heart lay hold of my words.’” The company of the disciples was the household of Christ, and he himself administered all parts of the service of God with them and among them (Luke 22:15). To this purpose74 Augustine says, “The master of the family in a way, and in his measure, performs the duty of a churchman, or bishop, within his house.”

II. To bring his family to the church or congregation on the Sabbath day; to see that they behave themselves there reverently; and when the public services are ended and the congregation is dismissed, to take an account of what they have heard, so that they may profit in knowledge and obedience. Acts 10:24: “The following day he arrived in Caesarea, where Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.” And v. 33: “Now then,” says Cornelius to Peter, “we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has instructed you to tell us.” Job 1:5: “And when the days of feasting were over, Job would send for his children to purify them, rising early in the morning to offer burnt offerings,” etc. 2 Kgs 4:23: “‘Why would you go to him today?’ he replied. ‘It is not a New Moon or a Sabbath.’” For this very reason the fourth commandment is given first of all and chiefly to the master of the family, so that he might see the Sabbath kept and be a principal doer in all parts of God’s worship on it. Exod 20:10: “On it you must not do any work—neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates.”

Nor is this care of his tied only to the Sabbath. On other days besides, he ought to see that those of his household go, as far as lies in him, to places where the word of God is preached. Commendable in this case was the practice of Mary the sister of Martha, who, when Christ came to her house, is said to have “sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message” (Luke 10:39).

III. To provide food, drink and clothing for his family, and that they may live a quiet and peaceable life (1 Tim 5:8). Prov 27:26: “The lambs will provide you with clothing, and the goats with the price of a field.” And v. 27: “You will have plenty of goats’ milk to feed you—food for your household and nourishment for your maidservants.” 1 Cor 9:9: “‘Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.’ Is it about oxen that God is concerned? Isn’t He actually speaking on our behalf?” Matt 13:52: “Every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old.”

IV. To keep order and to exercise discipline in his house, and that in this manner.

In case of offense, when a capital crime is committed which incurs public censure, he is not to punish it himself, but to bring the offender to the civil magistrate and inform him of the offender’s fault, so that the offender may receive what he deserves. This course was established by the judicial law which God gave to Moses for his direction in criminal cases among the Israelites. Deut 21:18, 19, 20: “If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who does not obey his father and mother and does not listen to them when disciplined, his father and mother are to lay hold of him and bring him to the elders of his city, to the gate of his hometown, and say to the elders, ‘This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey us. He is a glutton and a drunkard.’” Again, Deut 13:6: “If your very own brother, or your son or daughter, or the wife you embrace, or your closest friend secretly entices you, saying, ‘Let us go and worship other gods’ (which neither you nor your fathers have known …), you must not yield to him or listen to him. Show him no pity, and do not spare him or shield him.” Zech 13:3: “And if anyone still prophesies, his father and mother who bore him will say to him, ‘You shall not remain alive, because you have spoken falsely in the name of the Lord.’ When he prophesies, his father and mother who bore him will pierce him through.”

If the fault is of a lesser nature and smaller by comparison, the master of the family ought to proceed by private censure against the offending party: at times by admonition, at other times by correction and chastisement, according to the quality of the offense and the condition and state of the person. Lev 19:17: “Directly rebuke your neighbor, and do not let him go on in sin.” Matt 18:15: “If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. … But if he will not listen, take one or two others along.” Prov 29:17: “Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul.”

When admonitions and corrections will not prevail, the party must be brought before the ministers and governors of the Church, so that they may censure him. Matt 18:17: “If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church.” And the apostle James gives order that the ministers of the Church should come to those who are sick and pray for them (Jas 5:14). If they are to do this in a case of sickness, then they are also to be sought out for redress in a case of error and offense committed.

But when none of all these means will do good, if the party is a servant, his master may, and ought to, remove him. Ps 101:7: “No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who tells lies shall stand in my presence.” John 8:35: “A servant does not remain in the house forever.”

V. To give hospitality to those who are strangers and not of the family, if they are Christians and believers, but especially to the ministers of the Word. Rom 12:13: “Practice hospitality.” Heb 13:2: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it.” The woman of Shunem and her husband performed this duty for the prophet Elisha. 2 Kgs 4:10: “Please let us make a small room upstairs and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp for him. Then when he comes to us, he can stay there.” These are the duties.

Here it may be asked whether the master of a family is always and necessarily bound to do all these things in his own person.

I answer: if there is just and necessary cause, either because of his own inability or because of public employment in a lawful calling, by which he is hindered so that at some times he cannot do any of them himself, it is lawful for him to have and use a deputy. Our Savior Christ teaches this in effect when he says, “Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom the master has put in charge of his household, to give the others their food at the proper time?” (Matt 24:45). So Abraham had a steward of his house, Eliezer of Damascus (Gen 15:2). And he carried out the weightiest matters that concerned the establishment and continuance of his family, not by himself, but by his steward, namely the choice of a wife for his son Isaac. Gen 24:2: “So Abraham instructed the chief servant of his household, who managed all he owned, ‘Place your hand under my thigh,’” etc. So Pharaoh king of Egypt had Joseph. Gen 39:4: “Joseph found favor in his sight and became his personal attendant. He put him in charge of his household and entrusted him with everything he owned.”

74. In Ioan. tract. 51. in fine.

18. Of the Mistress of the Family, or Goodwife of the House

The goodwife, or mistress of the house, is a person who gives help and assistance in government to the master of the family. For he is, as it were, the prince and chief ruler; she is his associate, not only in office and authority, but also in advice and counsel to him. 1 Kgs 17:17: “Later, the son of the woman who was the wife, or75 mistress of the house, became ill.”

Her duty is twofold.

First, to govern the house, as far as concerns her, in her place. 1 Tim 5:14: “So I want the younger women to marry … and govern their households.” And this she does in three ways.

  1. By occupying herself in some profitable work for the good of her charge. Prov 31:13: “She selects wool and flax and works with eager hands.”
  2. By appointing her maids their work and overseeing them in it. Verse 15: “She rises while it is still night to provide food for her household and portions for her maidservants.”
  3. By directing her children and servants in wisdom, partly by instruction, partly by admonition when there is need. Verse 26: “She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue.” v. 28: “Her children rise up and call her blessed,” etc. Titus 2:5: “to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households,” etc. Acts 18:26: Priscilla, in her house, with Aquila, instructed Apollos in what he lacked, explaining to him “the way of God more accurately.” Gregory Nazianzen, in an oration made for his father, says “that his mother was not only a helper, but also a teacher or instructor, and guide to his father in matters of religion and godliness.”

The second duty is to give the portion of food to her family, or have it given, in due season. Prov 31:15: “She rises while it is still night to provide food for her household.” So Rebekah did in her house. Gen 27:9: “Go out to the flock and bring me two choice young goats, so that I can make them into a tasty dish for your father—the kind he loves.”

Question. May the mistress of the house give away and bestow the goods belonging to the family without the consent of the master of the house?

Answer. I. There are some things which are her own, and not part of the dowry which she brought to her husband. These she may claim as her own, because either they were reserved when the match was made between them, or else they belong to her alone by their mutual consent. And of these she may lawfully give without her husband’s knowledge. II. The goods which are common to them both are of another nature. These she may not bestow without his allowance, either express or at least general and implied, especially when the giving of them does, or in likelihood may, grow to the hindrance and harm of the state of the family.

75. [Bagnalath babbaijth.] Domina domus.
